nigged.c: nigged nigged (nĭgd), n. [Prov. E. nig to clip money.] (Masonry) Hammer-dressed; -- said of building stone.

nigger.c: nigger nig"ger (?), n. A negro; -- in vulgar derision or depreciation. It is usually intended and interpreted as highly insulting and vulgar. [Low, deprecatory, and vulgar]

niggerhead.c: Niggerhead Nig"ger*head` (?), n. A strong black chewing tobacco, usually in twisted plug form; negro head. [archaic]

niggle.c: Niggle Nig"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Niggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Niggling (?).] [Dim. of Prov. E. nig to clip money; cf. also Prov. E. nig a small piece.] To trifle with; to deceive; to mock. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
Niggle Nig"gle, v. i. 1. To trifle or play.
Niggle Nig"gle (?), v. t. 1. To use, spend, or do in a petty or trifling manner.

niggling.c: niggling nig"gling (?), n. Finicky or pottering work; specif. (Fine Arts), Minute and very careful workmanship in drawing, painting, or the like, esp. when bestowed on unimportant detail.

nigh.c: Nigh Nigh (nī), a. [Compar. Nigher (nī"ẽr); superl. Nighest, or Next (nĕkst).] [OE. nigh, neigh, neih, AS. neáh, nēh; akin to D. na, adv., OS. nāh, a., OHG. nāh, G. nah, a., nach to, after, Icel. nā (in comp.) nigh, Goth. nēhw, nēhwa, adv., nigh. Cf. Near, Neighbor, Next.] 1. Not distant or remote in place or time; near.
Nigh Nigh, adv. [AS. neáh, nēh. See Nigh, a.] 1. In a situation near in place or time, or in the course of events; near.
Nigh Nigh, v. t. & i. To draw nigh (to); to approach; to come near. [Obs.] Wyclif (Matt. iii. 2).
Nigh Nigh, prep. Near to; not remote or distant from. “was not this nigh shore?” Shak.

nighly.c: Nighly Nigh"ly, adv. In a near relation in place, time, degree, etc.; within a little; almost. [Obs.]

nighness.c: Nighness Nigh"ness, n. The quality or state of being nigh. [R.] “Nighness of blood.” Holished.

night.c: Night Night (nīt), n. [OE. night, niht, AS. neaht, niht; akin to D. nacht, OS. & OHG. naht, G. nacht, Icel. nōtt, Sw. natt, Dan. nat, Goth. nahts, Lith. naktis, Russ. noche, W. nos, Ir. nochd, L. nox, noctis, Gr. ny`x, nykto`s, Skr. nakta, nakti. √265. Cf. Equinox, Nocturnal.] 1. That part of the natural day when the sun is beneath the horizon, or the time from sunset to sunrise; esp., the time between dusk and dawn, when there is no light of the sun, but only moonlight, starlight, or artificial light.
Night lettergram Night letter { Night letter, Night lettergram }. See Letter, above.
Night terrors Night terrors. (Med.) A sudden awakening associated with a sensation of terror, occurring in children, esp. those of unstable nervous constitution.

nightblooming.c: Night-blooming Night"-bloom`ing (?), a. Blooming in the night.

nightcap.c: Nightcap Night"cap` (?), n. 1. A cap worn in bed to protect the head, or in undress.

nightertale.c: Nightertale Night"er*tale (?), n. [Cf. Icel. nāttarpel.] Period of night; nighttime. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nighteyed.c: Night-eyed Night"-eyed` (?), a. Capable of seeing at night; sharp-eyed. “Your night-eyed Tiberius.” B. Jonson.

nightfall.c: Nightfall Night"fall` (?), n. The close of the day; the arrival of the night; the period at and just after dusk. Swift.

nightfaring.c: Night-faring Night"-far`ing (?), a. Going or traveling in the night. Gay.

nightgown.c: Nightgown Night"gown` (?), n. A loose gown used for undress; also, a gown used for a sleeping garment.

nightingale.c: Nightingale Night"in*gale (?), n. [OE. nihtegale,nightingale, AS. nihtegale; niht night + galan to sing, akin to E. yell; cf. D. nachtegaal, OS. nahtigala, OHG. nahtigala, G. nachtigall, Sw. näktergal, Dan. nattergal. See Night, and Yell.] 1. (Zool.) A small, plain, brown and gray European song bird (Luscinia megarhynchos syn. Luscinia luscinia). It sings at night, and is celebrated for the sweetness of its song.

nightish.c: Nightish Night"ish, a. Of or pertaining to night.

nightjar.c: Nightjar Night"jar` (?), n. A goatsucker, esp. the European species. See Illust. of Goatsucker.

nightly.c: Nightly Night"ly, a. Of or pertaining to the night, or to every night; happening or done by night, or every night; as, nightly shades; he kept nightly vigils.
Nightly Night"ly, adv. At night; every night.

nightman.c: Nightman Night"man (nīt"măn), n.; pl. Nightmen (nīt"mĕn). One whose business is emptying privies by night.

nightmare.c: Nightmare Night"mare` (nīt"mâr`), n. [Night + mare incubus. See Mare incubus.] 1. A fiend or incubus formerly supposed to cause trouble in sleep. [archaic]

nightshade.c: Nightshade Night"shade` (?), n. [AS. nichtscadu.] (Bot.) A common name of many species of the genus Solanum, given esp. to the Solanum nigrum, or black nightshade, a low, branching weed with small white flowers and black berries reputed to be poisonous.

nightshirt.c: Nightshirt Night"shirt` (?), n. A kind of nightgown for men.

nighttime.c: Nighttime Night"time` (?), n. The time from dusk to dawn; -- opposed to daytime.

nigraniline.c: Nigraniline Ni*gran"i*line (? or?), n. [L. niger black + E. aniline.] (Chem.) The complex, nitrogenous, organic base and dyestuff called also aniline black.

nigrescent.c: Nigrescent Ni*gres"cent (?), a. [L. nigrescens, p. pr. of nigrescere to grow black, fr. niger black. See Negro.] Growing black; changing to a black color; approaching to blackness. Johnson.

nigrification.c: Nigrification Nig`ri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. nigrificare to blacken; niger black + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.] The act or process of making black. [R.] Johnson.

nigrine.c: Nigrine Ni"grine (?), n. [L. niger black: cf. F. nigrine.] (Min.) A ferruginous variety of rutile.

nigritic.c: Nigritic Ni*grit"ic (?), a. (Ethnol.) Pertaining to, or having the characteristics of, negroes, or of the Negritos, Papuans, and the Melanesian races; negritic.

nigritude.c: Nigritude Nig"ri*tude (?), n. [L. nigritudo, fr. niger black.] Blackness; the state of being black. Lamb.

nigrosine.c: Nigrosine Ni"gro*sine (? or?), n. [From L. niger black.] (Chem.) A dark blue dyestuff, of the induline group; -- called also azodiphenyl blue.

nihilism.c: Nihilism Ni"hil*ism (?), n. [L. nihil nothing: cf. F. nihilisme. See Annihilate.] 1. Nothingness; nihility.

nihilist.c: Nihilist Ni"hil*ist, n. [Cf. F. nihiliste. See Nihilism.] 1. One who advocates the doctrine of nihilism; one who believes or teaches that nothing can be known, or asserted to exist.

nihilistic.c: Nihilistic Ni`hil*is"tic (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or characterized by, nihilism.

nihility.c: Nihility Ni*hil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. nihilité. See Nihilism.] Nothingness; a state of being nothing.

nil.c: Nil Nil (?). [See Nill, v. t.] Will not. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Nil Nil, n. & a. [L., a contr. of nihil.] Nothing; of no account; worthless; -- a term often used for canceling, in accounts or bookkeeping. A. J. Ellis.

nile.c: Nile Nile (nīl), n. [L. Nilus, Gr. Nei^los.] The great river of Egypt.

nill.c: Nill Nill (nĭl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nilled (nĭld); p. pr. & vb. n. Nilling.] [AS. nilan, nyllan; ne not + willan to will. See No, and Will.] Not to will; to refuse; to reject. [Obs.]
Nill Nill, v. i. To be unwilling; to refuse to act.
Nill Nill, n. [Cf. Ir. & Gael. neul star, light. Cf. Nebula.] 1. Shining sparks thrown off from melted brass.

nilometer.c: Nilometer Ni*lom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.?; Nei^los the Nile +? measure: cf. F. nilomètre.] An instrument for measuring the rise of water in the Nile during its periodical flood.

niloscope.c: Niloscope Ni"lo*scope (?), n. [Gr. Nei^los; Nei^los the Nile +? to observe.] A Nilometer.

nilotic.c: Nilotic Ni*lot"ic (?), a. [L. Niloticus, fr. Nilus the Nile, Gr.?: cf. F. nilotique.] Of or pertaining to the river Nile; as, the Nilotic crocodile.

nilt.c: Nilt Nilt (?). [Contr. fr. ne wilt.] Wilt not. [Obs.]

nim.c: Nim Nim (nĭm), v. t. [imp. Nam (näm) or Nimmed (nĭmd); p. p. Nomen (nō"mein) or Nome (nōm).] [AS. niman. √7. Cf. Nimble.] To take; to steal; to filch. [Obs.]

nimbiferous.c: Nimbiferous Nim*bif"er*ous (?), a. [L. nimbifer; nimbus a cloud + ferre to bear.] Serving to bring clouds or stormy weather.

nimble.c: Nimble Nim"ble (nĭm"b'l), a. [Compar. Nimbler (nĭm"blẽr); superl. Nimblest (nĭm"blĕst).] [OE. nimel, prob. orig., quick at seizing, fr. nimen to take, AS. niman; akin to D. nemen, G. nehmen, OHG. neman, Icel. nema, Goth. nima, and prob. to Gr. ne`mein to distribute. √ 7. Cf. Nomand, Numb.] Light and quick in motion; moving with ease and celerity; lively; swift.

nimbleness.c: Nimbleness Nim"ble*ness, n. The quality of being nimble; lightness and quickness in motion; agility; swiftness.

nimbly.c: Nimbly Nim"bly, adv. In a nimble manner; with agility; with light, quick motion.

nimbose.c: Nimbose Nim*bose" (?), a. [L. nimbosus, fr. nimbus cloud.] Cloudy; stormy; tempestuous.

nimbus.c: Nimbus Nim"bus (?), n.; pl. L. Nimbi (#), E. Nimbuses (#). [L., a rain storm, a rain cloud, the cloudshaped which enveloped the gods when they appeared on earth.] 1. (Fine Arts) A circle, or disk, or any indication of radiant light around the heads of divinities, saints, and sovereigns, upon medals, pictures, etc.; a halo. See Aureola, and Glory, n., 5.

nimiety.c: Nimiety Ni*mi"e*ty (?), n. [L. nimietas, fr. nimius, a., nimis, adv., too much.] State of being in excess. [R.]

nimious.c: Nimious Nim"i*ous (?), a. [L. nimius.] Excessive; extravagant; inordinate. [Obs.]

nin.c: nin nin (?). [Fr. ne in.] Not in. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nincompoop.c: nincompoop nin"com*poop (?), n. [A corruption of non compos.] A fool; a silly or stupid person. [Law]

nine.c: nine nine (nīn), a. [OE. nine, nihen, AS. nigon, nigan; akin to D. & LG. negen, OS. & OFries. nigun, OHG. niun, G. neun, Icel. nīu, sw. nio, Dan. ni, Goth. niun, Ir. & Gael. naoi, W. naw, L. novem, Gr. 'enne`a, Skr. navan; of unknown origin. √307. Cf. Novembeer.] Eight and one more; one less than ten; as, nine miles.
Nine Nine, n. 1. The number greater than eight by a unit; nine units or objects.

ninebark.c: Nine-bark Nine"-bark` (?), n. (Bot.) A white-flowered rosaceous shrub (Neillia opulifolia, or Spiraea opulifolia), common in the Northern United States. The bark separates into many thin layers, whence the name.

nineholes.c: Nineholes Nine"holes` (?), n. pl. A game in which nine holes are made in the ground, into which a ball is bowled.

ninekiller.c: Nine-killer Nine"-kill`er (?), n. [So called because it is believed to kill and impale on thorns nine birds, etc., in succession.] (Zool.) The northern butcher bird.

ninepence.c: Ninepence Nine"pence (?), n.; pl. Ninepences (?). 1. An old English silver coin, worth nine pence.

ninepins.c: Ninepins Nine"pins (?), n. pl. A game played with nine pins, or pieces of wood, set on end, at which a wooden ball is bowled to knock them down; bowling.

ninescore.c: Ninescore Nine"score` (?), a. Nine times twenty, or one hundred and eighty. -- n. The product of nine times twenty; ninescore units or objects.

nineteen.c: Nineteen Nine"teen` (?), a. [AS. nigontȳne, nigontēne. See Nine, and Ten.] Nine and ten; eighteen and one more; one less than twenty; as, nineteen months.
Nineteen Nine"teen`, n. 1. The number greater than eighteen by a unit; the sum of ten and nine; nineteen units or objects.

nineteenth.c: Nineteenth Nine"teenth` (?), a. [Cf. AS. nigonteóða.] 1. Following the eighteenth and preceding the twentieth; coming after eighteen others.
Nineteenth Nine"teenth`, n. 1. The quotient of a unit divided by nineteen; one of nineteen equal parts of anything.

ninetieth.c: Ninetieth Nine"ti*eth (?), a. 1. Next in order after the eighty-ninth.
Ninetieth Nine"ti*eth, n. 1. The quotient of a unit divided by ninety; one of ninety equal parts of anything.

ninety.c: Ninety Nine"ty (?), a. [See Nine, and cf. Forty.] Nine times ten; eighty-nine and one more; as, ninety men.
Ninety Nine"ty, n.; pl. Nineties (?). 1. The sum of nine times ten; the number greater by a unit than eighty-nine; ninety units or objects.

ninny.c: Ninny Nin"ny (?), n.; pl. Ninnies (#). [Cf. It. ninno, ninna, a baby, Sp. niño, niña, child, infant, It. ninna, ninna nanna, lullably, prob. fr. ni, na, as used in singing a child to sleep.] A fool; a simpleton. Shak.

ninnyhammer.c: Ninnyhammer Nin"ny*ham`mer (?), n. A simpleton; a silly person. [Colloq.] Addison.

ninth.c: Ninth Ninth (?), a. [From Nine; cf. AS. nigoða.] 1. Following the eight and preceding the tenth; coming after eight others.
Ninth Ninth, n. 1. The quotient of one divided by nine; one of nine equal parts of a thing; the next after the eighth.

ninthly.c: Ninthly Ninth"ly, adv. In the ninth place.

niobate.c: Niobate Ni"o*bate (?), n. [See Niobium.] (Chem.) Same as Columbate.

niobe.c: Niobe Ni"o*be (?), n. [L. Nioba, Niobe, Gr.?.] (Class. Myth.) The daughter of Tantalus, and wife of Amphion, king of Thebes. Her pride in her children provoked Apollo and Diana, who slew them all. Niobe herself was changed by the gods into stone.

niobium.c: niobium ni*o"bi*um (?), n. [NL., fr. L. & E. Niobe.] (Chem.) The chemical element of atomic number 41. Chemical symbol Nb. Atomic weight 92.91. Previously called columbium. See also Columbium.

niopo.c: Niopo Ni*o"po (?), n. A kind of snuff prepared by the natives of Venezuela from the roasted seeds of a leguminous tree (Piptadenia peregrina), thence called niopo tree.

nip.c: Nip Nip (?), n. [LG. & D. nippen to sip; akin to Dan. nippe, G. nippen.] A sip or small draught; esp., a draught of intoxicating liquor; a dram.

Nip Nip, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nipped (?), less properly Nipt; p. pr. & vb. n. Nipping (?).] [OE. nipen; cf. D. niipen to pinch, also knippen to nip, clip, pinch, snap, knijpen to pinch, LG. knipen, G. kneipen, kneifen, to pinch, cut off, nip, Lith. knebti.] 1. To catch and inclose or compress tightly between two surfaces, or points which are brought together or closed; to pinch; to close in upon.
Nip Nip, n. 1. A seizing or closing in upon; a pinching; as, in the northern seas, the nip of masses of ice.

nipper.c: Nipper Nip"per (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, nips.

nipperkin.c: Nipperkin Nip"per*kin, n. [See 1st Nip.] A small cup. [Obs.]

nippers.c: Nippers Nip"pers (?), n. pl. [From 2d Nip.] 1. Small pinchers for holding, breaking, or cutting.

nipping.c: Nipping Nip"ping (?), a. Biting; pinching; painful; destructive; as, a nipping frost; a nipping wind.

nippingly.c: Nippingly Nip"ping*ly, adv. In a nipping manner.

nippitate.c: Nippitate Nip"pi*tate (?), a. [Cf. 1st Nip.] Peculiarly strong and good; -- said of ale or liquor. [Old Cant]

nippitato.c: Nippitato Nip`pi*ta"to (?), n. Strong liquor. [Old Cant] Beau. & Fl.

nipple.c: Nipple Nip"ple (nĭp"p'l), n. [Formerly neble, a dim. of neb. See Neb, Nib.] 1. (Anat.) The protuberance through which milk is drawn from the breast or mamma; the mammilla; a teat; a pap.

nipplewort.c: Nipplewort Nip"ple*wort` (nĭp"p'l*wûrt`), n. (Bot.) A yellow-flowered composite herb (Lampsana communis), formerly used as an external application to the nipples of women; -- called also dock-cress.

nirvana.c: Nirvana ‖Nir*va"na (?), n. [Skr. nirvāṇa.] In the Buddhist system of religion, the final emancipation of the soul from transmigration, and consequently a beatific enfrachisement from the evils of worldly existence, as by annihilation or absorption into the divine. See Buddhism.

nis.c: Nis Nis (?). [From ne is.] Is not. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nisan.c: Nisan ‖Ni"san (?), n. [Heb. nīsān.] The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, formerly answering nearly to the month of April, now to March, of the Christian calendar. See Abib.

nisey.c: Nisey Ni"sey (?), n.; pl. Nyseys. A simpleton. [Obs.]

nisi.c: Nisi ‖Ni"si (?), conj. [L.] Unless; if not; -- used mostly in law.

niste.c: Niste Nis"te (?). [Contr. from ne wiste.] Wist not; knew not. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nisus.c: Nisus ‖Ni"sus (?), n. [L., fr. niti, p. p. nisus, to strive.] 1. A striving; an effort; a conatus.

nit.c: Nit Nit (nĭt), n. [AS. hnitu; akin to D. neet, G. niss, OHG. niz; cf. Gr. koni`s, koni`dos, Icel. gnit, Sw. gnet, Dan. gnid, Russ. & Pol. gnida, Bohem. hnida, W. nedd.] (Zool.) The egg of a louse or other small insect.

nitency.c: Nitency Ni"ten*cy (?), n. [L. nitens, p. pr. of nitere to shine.] Brightness; luster. [R.]
Nitency Ni"ten*cy, n. [From L. nitens, p. pr. of niti to strive.] Endeavor; effort; tendency. [R.] Boyle.

nitre.c: Nitre Niter { Ni"ter, Ni"tre } (?), n. [F. nitre, L. nitrum native soda, natron, Gr.?; cf. Ar. nitūn, natrūn natron. Cf. Natron.] 1. (Chem.) A white crystalline semitransparent salt; potassium nitrate; saltpeter. See Saltpeter.

nitid.c: Nitid Nit"id (?), a. [L. nitidus, fr. nitere. See 3d Neat.] 1. Bright; lustrous; shining. [R.] Boyle.

nitranilic.c: Nitranilic Ni`tra*nil"ic (?), a. [Nitro- + chloranil + -ic.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, a complex organic acid produced as a white crystalline substance by the action of nitrous acid on hydroquinone.

nitraniline.c: Nitraniline Ni*tran"i*line (? or?), n. [Nitro- + aniline.] (Chem.) Any one of a series of nitro derivatives of aniline; nitroaniline. In general they are yellow crystalline substances.

nitrate.c: Nitrate Ni"trate (?), n. [Cf. F. nitrate.] (Chem.) A salt of nitric acid.

nitrated.c: Nitrated Ni"tra*ted (?), a. 1. (Chem.) Combined, or impregnated, with nitric acid, or some of its compounds.

nitratine.c: Nitratine Ni"tra*tine (?), n. (Min.) A mineral occurring in transparent crystals, usually of a white, sometimes of a reddish gray, or lemon-yellow, color; native sodium nitrate. It is used in making nitric acid and for manure. Called also soda niter.

nitriary.c: Nitriary Ni"tri*a*ry (?), n. [See Niter.] An artificial bed of animal matter for the manufacture of niter by nitrification. See Nitrification, 2.

nitric.c: Nitric Ni"tric (?), a. [Cf. F. nitrique. See Niter.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or containing, nitrogen; specifically, designating any one of those compounds in which, as contrasted with nitrous compounds, the element has a higher valence; as, nitric oxide; nitric acid.

nitride.c: Nitride Ni"tride (? or?), n. [fromNitrogen.] (Chem.) A binary compound of nitrogen with a more metallic element or radical; as, boric nitride.

nitriferous.c: Nitriferous Ni*trif"er*ous (?), a. [Niter + -ferous.] Bearing niter; yielding, or containing, niter.

nitrification.c: Nitrification Ni`tri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. nitrification. see Nitrify.] 1. (Chem.) (a) The act, process, or result of combining with nitrogen or some of its compounds. (b) The act or process of oxidizing nitrogen or its compounds so as to form nitrous or nitric acid.

nitrifier.c: Nitrifier Ni"tri*fi`er (?), n. (Chem.) An agent employed in nitrification.

nitrify.c: Nitrify Ni"tri*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nitrified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nitrifying (?).] [Niter + -fy: cf. F. nitrifer. See Niter.] (Chem.) To combine or impregnate with nitrogen; to convert, by oxidation, into nitrous or nitric acid; to subject to, or produce by, nitrification.

nitrile.c: Nitrile Ni"trile (? or?), n. [See Nitro-.] (Chem.) Any one of a series of compounds bearing the cyanide radical (-CN); particularly, one of those cyanides of alcohol radicals which, by boiling with acids or alkalies, produce a carboxyl acid, with the elimination of the nitrogen as ammonia.

nitrite.c: Nitrite Ni"trite (?), n. [Cf. F. nitrite. See Niter.] (Chem.) A salt or ester of nitrous acid; a compound bearing the -NO2 radical.

nitro.c: nitro- ni"tro- (?) pref. 1. A combining form or an adjective denoting the presence of niter.

nitrobenzene.c: Nitrobenzene Ni`tro*ben"zene (? or?), n. [Nitro- + benzene.] (Chem.) A yellow aromatic liquid (C6H5.NO2), produced by the action of nitric acid on benzene, and called from its odor imitation oil of bitter almonds, or essence of mirbane. It is used in perfumery, and is manufactured in large quantities in the preparation of aniline. Fornerly called also nitrobenzol.

nitrobenzole.c: Nitrobenzole Nitrobenzol { Ni`tro*ben"zol, Ni`tro*ben"zole, (? or?) }, n. See Nitrobenzene.

nitrocalcite.c: Nitrocalcite Ni`tro*cal"cite (?), n. [Nitro- + calcite.] (Min.) Nitrate of calcium, a substance having a grayish white color, occuring in efflorescences on old walls, and in limestone caves, especially where there exists decaying animal matter.

nitrocarbol.c: Nitrocarbol Ni`tro*car"bol (?), n. [Nitro- + carbon + L. oleum oil.] (Chem.) See Nitromethane.

nitrocellulose.c: Nitrocellulose Ni`tro*cel"lu*lose` (?), n. [Nitro- + cellulose.] (Chem.) See Gun cotton, under Gun.

nitrochloroform.c: Nitro-chloroform Ni`tro-chlo"ro*form (?), n. [Nitro- + chloroform.] (Chem.) Same as Chlorpicrin.

nitroform.c: Nitroform Ni"tro*form (?), n. [Nitro- + formyl.] (Chem.) A nitro derivative of methane, analogous to chloroform, obtained as a colorless oily or crystalline substance, CH.(NO2)3, quite explosive, and having well-defined acid properties.

nitrogelatin.c: Nitrogelatin Ni`tro*gel"a*tin (?), n. [Nitro- + gelatin.] An explosive consisting of gun cotton and camphor dissolved in nitroglycerin. [Written also nitrogelatine.]

nitrogen.c: Nitrogen Ni`tro*gen (nī"tro*jĕn), n. [L. nitrum natron + -gen: cf. F. nitrogène. See Niter.] (Chem.) A colorless nonmetallic element of atomic number 7, tasteless and odorless, comprising four fifths of the atmosphere by volume in the form of molecular nitrogen (N2). It is chemically very inert in the free state, and as such is incapable of supporting life (hence the name azote still used by French chemists); but it forms many important compounds, such as ammonia, nitric acid, the cyanides, etc, and is a constituent of all organized living tissues, animal or vegetable. Symbol N. Atomic weight 14.007. It was formerly regarded as a permanent noncondensible gas, but was liquefied in 1877 by Cailletet of Paris, and Pictet of Geneva, and boils at -195.8 ° C at atmospheric pressure. Liquid nitrogen is used as a refrigerant to store delicate materials, such as bacteria, cells, and other biological materials.

nitrogenize.c: Nitrogenize Ni"tro*gen*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nitrogenized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nitrogenizing.] (Chem.) To combine, or impregnate, with nitrogen or its compounds.

nitrogenous.c: Nitrogenous Ni*trog"e*nous (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or resembling, nitrogen; as, a nitrogenous principle; nitrogenous compounds.

nitroglycerine.c: Nitroglycerine Nitroglycerin Ni`tro*glyc"er*in, Ni`tro*glyc"er*ine (nī`tro*glĭs"ẽr*ĭn), n. [Nitro- + glycerin.] (Chem.) A liquid appearing like a heavy oil, colorless or yellowish, and consisting of a mixture of several glycerin salts of nitric acid, and hence more properly called glycerin nitrate; also called trinitroglycerin and glyceryl trinitrate. It is made by the action of nitric acid on glycerin in the presence of sulphuric acid. It is extremely unstable and terribly explosive. A very dilute solution is used in medicine as a neurotic under the name of glonion. [Written also nitroglycerine.]

nitrohydrochloric.c: Nitrohydrochloric Ni`tro*hy`dro*chlo"ric (?), a. [Nitro- + hydrochloric.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or containing, nitric and hydrochloric acids.

nitrol.c: Nitrol Ni"trol (?), n. (Chem.) Any one of a series of hydrocarbons containing the nitro and the nitroso or isonitroso group united to the same carbon atom.

nitroleum.c: Nitroleum Ni*tro"le*um (?), n. [NL., fr. L. nitrum natron + oleum oil.] (Chem.) Nitroglycerin.

nitrolic.c: Nitrolic Ni*trol"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of, derived from, or designating, a nitrol; as, a nitrolic acid.

nitromagnesite.c: Nitromagnesite Ni`tro*mag"ne*site (?), n. [Nitro- + magnesite.] (Chem.) Nitrate of magnesium, a saline efflorescence closely resembling nitrate of calcium.

nitrometer.c: Nitrometer Ni*trom"e*ter (?), n. [Nitro- + -meter: cf. F. nitromètre.] (Chem.) An apparatus for determining the amount of nitrogen or some of its compounds in any substance subjected to analysis; an azotometer.

nitromethane.c: Nitromethane Ni`tro*meth"ane (?), n. [Nitro- + methane.] (Chem.) A nitro derivative of methane (CH3.NO2), obtained as a mobile liquid; -- called also nitrocarbol. It has been used as a rocket fuel and as a gasoline additive to add power to the fuel, especially in racing cars.

nitromuriatic.c: Nitromuriatic Ni`tro*mu`ri*at"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. nitromuriatique. See Nitro-, and Muriatic.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or composed of, nitric acid and muriatic acid; nitrohydrochloric. See Nitrohydrochloric.

nitrophnol.c: Nitrophnol Ni`tro*ph"nol (?), n. [Nitro- + phenol.] (Chem.) Any one of a series of nitro derivatives of phenol. They are yellow oily or crystalline substances and have well-defined acid properties, as picric acid.

nitroprussic.c: Nitroprussic Ni`tro*prus"sic (? or?), a. [Nitro- + prussic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, a complex acid called nitroprussic acid, obtained indirectly by the action of nitric acid on potassium ferrocyanide (yellow prussiate), as a red crystalline unstable substance. It forms salts called nitroprussides, which give a rich purple color with alkaline sulphides.

nitroquinol.c: Nitroquinol Ni`tro*qui"nol (?), n. [Nitro- + quine + -ol.] (Chem.) A hypothetical nitro derivative of quinol or hydroquinone, not known in the free state, but forming a well defined series of derivatives.

nitrosaccharin.c: Nitrosaccharin Ni`tro*sac"cha*rin (?), n. [Nitro- + saccharin.] (Chem.) An explosive nitro derivative of certain sugars, analogous to nitroglycerin, gun cotton, etc.

nitrosalicylic.c: Nitrosalicylic Ni`tro*sal`i*cyl"ic (?), a. [Nitro- + salicylic.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, a nitro derivative of salicylic acid, called also anilic acid.

nitroso.c: Nitroso- Ni*tro"so- (? or?). (Chem.) A prefix (also used adjectively) designating the group or radical -NO, called the nitroso group, or its compounds.

nitrosyl.c: Nitrosyl Ni*tro"syl (?), n. [Nitroso- + -yl.] (Chem.) The radical -NO, called also the nitroso group. The term is sometimes loosely used to designate certain nitro compounds; as, nitrosyl sulphuric acid. Used also adjectively.

nitrosylic.c: Nitrosylic Ni`tro*syl"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or containing, nitrosyl; as, nitrosylic acid.

nitrous.c: Nitrous Ni"trous (?), a. [L. nitrosus full of natron: cf. F. nitreux. See Niter.] 1. Of, pertaining to, or containing, niter; of the quality of niter, or resembling it.

nitroxyl.c: Nitroxyl Ni*trox"yl (?), n. [Nitro- + oxygen + -yl.] (Chem.) The group -NO2, usually called the nitro group.

nitrum.c: Nitrum ‖Ni"trum (?), n. [L., natron. See Niter.] (Old Chem.) Niter.

nitryl.c: Nitryl Ni"tryl (?), n. [Nitro- + -yl.] (Chem.) A name sometimes given to the nitro group or radical.

nitter.c: Nitter Nit"ter (?), n. [From Nit.] (Zool.) The horse louse; an insect that deposits nits on horses.

nittings.c: Nittings Nit"tings (?), n. pl. [Prob. from Nit.] (Mining) The refuse of good ore. Raymond.

nitty.c: Nitty Nit"ty (?), a. Full of nits. B. Jonson.
Nitty Nit"ty, a. [L. nitidus. See Nitid.] Shining; elegant; spruce. [Obs.] “O sweet, nitty youth.” Marston.

nival.c: Nival Ni"val (?), a. [L. nivalis, fr. nix, nivis, snow.] Abounding with snow; snowy. [Obs.] Johnson.

niveous.c: Niveous Niv"e*ous (?), a. [L. niveus, fr. nix, nivis, snow.] Snowy; resembling snow; partaking of the qualities of snow. Sir T. Browne.

nivose.c: Nivose ‖Ni`vose" (?), n. [F., fr. L. nix. nivis, snow.] The fourth month of the French republican calendar [1792-1806]. It commenced December 21, and ended January 19. See Vendémiaire.

nix.c: Nix Nix (?), n.; fem. Nixe (?). [G. Cf. 1st Nick.] (Teut. Myth.) One of a class of water spirits, commonly described as of a mischievous disposition.

nixie.c: Nixie clerk Nixie clerk. A post-office clerk in charge of the nixies.

nizam.c: Nizam ‖Ni*zam" (?), n. [Hind. & Ar. nizām order, a ruler, fr. Ar. nazama arrange, govern.] The title of the native sovereigns of Hyderabad, in India, since 1719.
Nizam ‖Ni*zam" (?), n.; pl. Nizam. [Turk. nizām.] A regular soldier of the Turkish army. See Army organization, above.

no.c: No No (nō), a. [OE. no, non, the same word as E. none; cf. E. a, an. See None.] Not any; not one; none; as, yes, we have no bananas; -- often used as a quantifier.

No No, adv. [OE. no, na, AS. nā; ne not + ā ever. AS. ne is akin to OHG. ni, Goth. ni, Russ. ne, Ir., Gael. & W. ni, L. ne, Gr. nh (in comp.), Skr. na, and also to E. prefix un-. √ 193. See Aye, and cf. Nay, Not, Nice, Nefarious.] Nay; not; not at all; not in any respect or degree; -- a word expressing negation, denial, or refusal. Before or after another negative, no is emphatic.
No No (nō), n.; pl. Noes (nōz). 1. A refusal by use of the word no; a denial.
No way Noways Noway { No"way` (?), No"ways` (?), No" way` } adv. [No, a. + way. Cf. -wards.] In no manner or degree; not at all; nowise.

noachian.c: Noachian No*a"chi*an (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to the patriarch Noah, or to his time.

noah.c: Noah No"ah (?), prop. n. [Heb. Nōakh rest.] A patriarch of Biblical history, in the time of the Deluge.

nob.c: Nob Nob, n. [Abbrev. fr. noble.] A person in a superior position in life; a nobleman. [Slang]

nobbily.c: Nobbily Nob"bi*ly (?), adv. In a nobby manner. [Slang]

nobbler.c: Nobbler Nob"bler (?), n. A dram of spirits. [Australia]

nobby.c: Nobby Nob"by (?), a. [From 2d Nob.] Stylish; modish; elegant; showy; aristocratic; fashionable. [Slang]

nobel.c: Nobel prize No*bel" prize (?) n.; pl. No*bel" prizes. Prizes for the encouragement of men and women who work for the interests of humanity, established by the will of Alfred B. Nobel (1833-1896), the Swedish inventor of dynamite, who left his entire estate for this purpose. They are awarded yearly for what is regarded as the most important work during the year in physics, chemistry, medicine or physiology, idealistic literature, and service in the interest of peace. The prizes, averaging $40,000 each, were first awarded in 1901. The monetary value of the awards have increased each year, to near one million U. S. dollars by the end of the 20th century.

noberts.c: Nobert's lines No"bert's lines (?). [After F. A. Nobert, German manufacturer in Pomerania.] Fine lines ruled on glass in a series of groups of different closeness of line, and used to test the power of a microscope.

nobiliary.c: Nobiliary No*bil"ia*ry (?), a. [F. nobiliare. See Noble.] Of or pertaining to the nobility. Fitzed. Hall.
Nobiliary No*bil"ia*ry, n. A history of noble families.

nobilify.c: Nobilify No*bil"i*fy (?), v. t. [L. nobilis noble + -fy.] To make noble; to nobiliate. [Obs.]

nobilis.c: Nobili's rings No"bi*li's rings (?). [After Leopoldo Nobili, an Italian physicist who first described them in 1826.] (Physics) Colored rings formed upon a metal plate by the electrolytic disposition of copper, lead peroxide, etc. They may be produced by touching with a pointed zinc rod a silver plate on which is a solution of copper sulphate.

nobilitate.c: Nobilitate No*bil"i*tate (?), v. t. [L. nobilitatus, p. p. of nobilitare.] To make noble; to ennoble; to exalt. [Obs.]

nobilitation.c: Nobilitation No*bil`i*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. OF. nobilitation.] The act of making noble. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

nobility.c: Nobility No*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. nobilitas: cf. OF. nobilité. See Noble.] 1. The quality or state of being noble; superiority of mind or of character; commanding excellence; eminence.

noble.c: Noble No"ble (?), a. [Compar. Nobler (?); superl. Noblest (?).] [F. noble, fr. L. nobilis that can be or is known, well known, famous, highborn, noble, fr. noscere to know. See know.] 1. Possessing eminence, elevation, dignity, etc.; above whatever is low, mean, degrading, or dishonorable; magnanimous; as, a noble nature or action; a noble heart.
Noble No"ble, n. 1. A person of rank above a commoner; a nobleman; a peer.
Noble No"ble, v. t. To make noble; to ennoble. [Obs.]

nobleman.c: Nobleman No"ble*man (?), n.; pl. Noblemen (?). One of the nobility; a noble; a peer; one who enjoys rank above a commoner, either by virtue of birth, by office, or by patent.

nobleminded.c: Noble-minded No"ble-mind`ed (?), a. Having a noble mind; of high moral or intellectual character; honorable; magnanimous. -- No"ble-mind`ed*ness, n.

nobleness.c: Nobleness No"ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being noble; greatness; dignity; magnanimity; elevation of mind, character, or station; nobility; grandeur; stateliness.

noblesse.c: Noblesse Nobless { No*bless", No*blesse" } (?; 277), n. [F. noblesse. See Noble.] 1. Dignity; greatness; noble birth or condition. [Obs.] Chaucer. Spenser. B. Jonson.

noblewoman.c: Noblewoman No"ble*wom`an (?), n.; pl. Noblewomen (?). A female of noble rank; a peeress.

nobley.c: Nobley No"bley (?), n. [OF. nobleie.] 1. The body of nobles; the nobility. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nobly.c: Nobly No"bly (?), adv. 1. Of noble extraction; as, nobly born or descended.

nobody.c: Nobody No"bod*y (?), n.; pl. Nobodies (#). [No, a. + body.] 1. No person; no one; not anybody.

nocake.c: Nocake No"cake (?), n. [Corrupted fr. Indian nookhik meal. Palfrey.] Indian corn parched, and beaten to powder, -- used for food by the Northern American Indians.

nocent.c: Nocent No"cent (nō"seint), a. [L. nocens, p. pr. of nocere to hurt. See Nuisance, Noxious.] 1. Doing hurt, or having a tendency to hurt; hurtful; mischievous; noxious; as, nocent qualities. I. Watts.
Nocent No"cent, n. A criminal. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

nocive.c: Nocive No"cive (?), a. [L. nocivus, fr. nocere to hurt.] Hurtful; injurious. [R.] Hooker.

nock.c: Nock Nock, v. t. To notch; to fit to the string, as an arrow; to string, as a bow. Chapman.

noctambulation.c: Noctambulation Noc*tam`bu*la"tion (?), n. [L. nox, noctis, night + ambulare to walk: cf. F. noctambulation.] Somnambulism; sleepwalking; walking in one's sleep. Quain.

noctambulist.c: Noctambulist Noc*tam"bu*list (?), n. A somnambulist; a sleepwalker.

noctambulo.c: Noctambulo Noc*tam"bu*lo (?), n. A noctambulist; a sleepwalker. [Obs.]

noctidial.c: Noctidial Noc*tid"i*al (?), a. [L. nox, noctos, night + dies day.] Comprising a night and a day; as, a noctidial day. [R.] Holder.

noctiferous.c: Noctiferous Noc*tif"er*ous (?), a. [L. noctifer; nox, noctis + ferre to bring.] Bringing night. [Obs.] Johnson.

noctilionid.c: Noctilionid Noc*til"i*o*nid (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) A South American bat of the genus Noctilio, having cheek pouches and large incisor teeth.

noctiluca.c: Noctiluca ‖Noc`ti*lu"ca (?), n.; pl. Noctilucae (#). [L. noctiluca something that shines by night, fr. nox, noctis, night + lucere to shine, lux light.] 1. (Old Chem.) That which shines at night; -- a fanciful name for phosphorus.

noctilucin.c: Noctilucin Noc*ti*lu"cin (?), n. (Zool.) A fatlike substance in certain marine animals, to which they owe their phosphorescent properties.

noctilucine.c: Noctilucine Noc`ti*lu"cine (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to Noctiluca.

noctilucous.c: Noctilucous Noc`ti*lu"cous (?), a. Shining in the night.

noctivagant.c: Noctivagant Noc*tiv"a*gant (?), a. [L. nox, noctis, night + vagans, p. pr. of vagari to wander about.] (Zool.) Going about in the night; night-wandering.

noctivagation.c: Noctivagation Noc*tiv`a*ga"tion (?), n. A roving or going about in the night. Gayton.

noctivagous.c: Noctivagous Noc*tiv"a*gous (?), a. [L. noctivagus; nox, noctis + vagus wandering.] Noctivagant.

noctograph.c: Noctograph Noc"to*graph (?), n. [L. nox, noctis, night + -graph.] 1. A kind of writing frame for the blind.

noctuary.c: Noctuary Noc"tu*a*ry (?; 135), n. [L. noctu by night.] A record of what passes in the night; a nightly journal; -- distinguished from diary. [R.] Addison.

noctuid.c: Noctuid Noc"tu*id (?), n. [From L. nox, noctis, night.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous moths of the family Noctuidae, or Noctuaelitae, as the cutworm moths, and armyworm moths; -- so called because they fly at night. -- a. Of or pertaining to the noctuids, or family Noctuidae.

noctule.c: Noctule Noc"tule (?; 135), n. [F., fr. L. noctua a night owl, fr. nox, noctis, night.] (Zool.) A large European bat (Vespertilio altivolans syn. Noctulina altivolans).

nocturn.c: Nocturn Noc"turn (?), n. [F. nocturne, fr. L. nocturnus. See Nocturnal, and cf. Nocturne.] 1. An office of devotion, or act of religious service, by night.

nocturnal.c: Nocturnal Noc*tur"nal (?), a. [L. nocturnalis, nocturnus, fr. nox, noctis, night. See Night, and cf. Nocturn.] 1. Of, pertaining to, done or occuring in, the night; as, nocturnal darkness, cries, expedition, etc.; -- opposed to diurnal. Dryden.
Nocturnal Noc*tur"nal, n. An instrument formerly used for taking the altitude of the stars, etc., at sea. I. Watts.

nocturne.c: Nocturne Noc*turne" (?), n. [F. See Nocturn.] (Mus.) A night piece, or serenade. The name is now used for a certain graceful and expressive form of instrumental composition, as the nocturne for orchestra in Mendelsohn's “Midsummer-Night's Dream” music.

nocument.c: Nocument Noc"u*ment (?), n. [LL. nocumentum, fr. L. nocere to hurt.] Harm; injury; detriment. [Obs.]

nocuous.c: Nocuous Noc"u*ous (?), a. [L. nocuus, fr. nocere to hurt.] Hurtful; noxious. [R.] -- Noc"u*ous*ly, adv. [R.]

nod.c: Nod Nod (nŏd), v. i. [OE. nodden; cf. OHG. knōtōn, genuotōn, to shake, and E. nudge.] 1. To bend or incline the upper part, with a quick motion; as, nodding plumes.
Nod Nod, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nodded (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nodding.] 1. To incline or bend, as the head or top; to make a motion of assent, of salutation, or of drowsiness with; as, to nod the head.
Nod Nod (nŏd), n. 1. A dropping or bending forward of the upper part or top of anything.

nodal.c: Nodal Nod"al (?), a. Of the nature of, or relating to, a node; as, a nodal point.

nodated.c: Nodated No"da*ted (?), a. [L. nodatus, p. p. of nodare to make knotty, fr. nodus knot. See Node.] Knotted.

nodation.c: Nodation No*da"tion (?), n. [L. nodatio knottiness.] Act of making a knot, or state of being knotted. [R.]

nodder.c: Nodder Nod"der (?), n. One who nods; a drowsy person.

nodding.c: Nodding Nod"ding (?), a. Curved so that the apex hangs down; having the top bent downward.

noddle.c: Noddle Nod"dle (?), n. [OE. nodil, nodle; perh. fr. nod, because the head is the nodding part of the body, or perh. akin to E. knot; cf. Prov. E. nod the nape of the neck.] 1. The head; also, noodle; -- used jocosely or contemptuously.

noddy.c: Noddy Nod"dy (?), n.; pl. Noddies (#). [Prob. fr. nod to incline the head, either as in assent, or from drowsiness.] 1. A simpleton; a fool. L'Estrange.

node.c: Node Node (nōd), n. [L. nodus; perh. akin to E. knot. Cf. Noose, Nowed.] 1. A knot, a knob; a protuberance; a swelling.

nodical.c: Nodical Nod"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to the nodes; from a node to the same node again; as, the nodical revolutions of the moon.

nodosarine.c: Nodosarine No`do*sa"rine (?), a. (Zool.) Resembling in form or structure a foraminiferous shell of the genus Nodosaria. -- n. (Zool.) A foraminifer of the genus Nodosaria or of an allied genus.

nodose.c: Nodose No*dose" (?), a. [L. nodosus, fr. nodus knot.] 1. Knotty; having numerous or conspicuous nodes.

nodosity.c: Nodosity No*dos"i*ty (?), n. [L. nodositas.] 1. The quality of being knotty or nodose; resemblance to a node or swelling; knottiness. Holland.

nodous.c: Nodous Nodosous { No*do"sous (?), No"dous (?) }, a. Nodose; knotty; knotted. [Obs.]

nodular.c: Nodular Nod"u*lar (nŏd"u*lẽr; 135), a. [Cf. F. nodulaire.] 1. Of or pertaining to a nodule or knot.

nodule.c: Nodule Nod"ule (nŏd"ul), n. [L. nodulus, dim. of nodus knot: cf. F. nodule.] A rounded mass or irregular shape; a little knot or lump.

noduled.c: Noduled Nod"uled (nŏd"uld), a. Having little knots or lumps.

nodulous.c: Nodulous Nodulose { Nod"u*lose` (nŏd"u*lōs`), Nod"u*lous (nŏd"u*lŭs), } a. (Biol.) Having small nodes or knots; diminutively nodose.

noel.c: Noel No"el (nō"ĕl), n. [F. noël, L. natalis birthday, fr. natalis natal. See Natal.] Same as Nowel.

noematachograph.c: Noematachograph No*e`ma*tach"o*graph (?), n. [Gr. no`hma the understanding + ta`chos swiftness + -graph.] An instrument for determining and registering the duration of more or less complex operations of the mind. Dunglison.

noematical.c: Noematical Noematic { No`e*mat"ic (?), No`e*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr. no`hma the understanding. See Noetic.] Of or pertaining to the understanding. [Obs.] Cudworth.

noemics.c: Noemics No*e"mics (?), n. [Gr. no`hma the understanding. See Noetic.] The science of the understanding; intellectual science.

noetian.c: Noetian No*e"tian (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of the followers of Noetus, who lived in the third century. He denied the distinct personality of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

noetical.c: Noetical Noetic { No*et"ic (?), No*et"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?, fr.? to perceive,? mind, intellect.] Of or pertaining to the intellect; intellectual.

nof.c: Nof Nof (?). [Contr. fr. ne of.] Not of; nor of. [Obs.]

nog.c: Nog Nog (?), n. [Abbrev. fr. noggin.] 1. A noggin.
Nog Nog, n. [Etymol. uncertain.] 1. A wooden block, of the size of a brick, built into a wall, as a hold for the nails of woodwork.
Nog Nog, v. t. [From 2d Nog.] 1. To fill in, as between scantling, with brickwork.

noggen.c: Noggen Nog"gen (?), a. [Prop., made of hemp, fr. Prov. E. nogs hemp.] Made of hemp; hence, hard; rough; harsh. [Obs.] Johnson.

noggin.c: Noggin Nog"gin (?), n. [Ir. noigin, or Gael. noigean. Cf. 1st Nog.] 1. A small mug or cup.

nogging.c: Nogging Nog"ging (?), n. [From Nog, v. t.] Rough brick masonry used to fill in the interstices of a wooden frame, in building.

noiance.c: Noiance Noi"ance (?), n. [Abbrev. fr. OE. anoiance.] [Written also noyance.] Annoyance. [Obs.] Tusser.

noie.c: Noie Noie (?), v. t. To annoy. See Noy. [Obs.]

noil.c: Noil Noil (?), n. [Prob. fr. Prov. E. oil, ile, ail, a beard of grain (OE. eil, AS. egl) combined with the indef. article, an oil becoming a noil.] A short or waste piece or knot of wool separated from the longer staple by combing; also, a similar piece or shred of waste silk.

noils.c: Noils Noils (?), n. pl. [Etymol. uncertain.] Waste and knots of wool removed by the comb; combings.

noint.c: Noint Noint (?), v. t. To anoint. [Obs.] Sir T. North.

noise.c: Noise Noise (?), n. [F. noise noisy strife, quarrel, brawl, fr. L. nausea seasickness, sickness, disgust. See Nausea.] 1. Sound of any kind.
Noise Noise, v. i. To sound; to make a noise. Milton.
Noise Noise, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Noised (?); p pr. & vb. n. Noising.] 1. To spread by rumor or report.

noiseless.c: Noiseless Noise"less, a. Making, or causing, no noise or bustle; without noise; silent; as, the noiseless foot of time.

noisette.c: Noisette Noi*sette" (?), n. (Bot.) A hybrid rose produced in 1817, by a French gardener, Noisette, of Charleston, South Carolina, from the China rose and the musk rose. It has given rise to many fine varieties, as the Lamarque, the Marechal (or Marshal) Niel, and the Cloth of gold. Most roses of this class have clustered flowers and are of vigorous growth. P. Henderson.

noisily.c: Noisily Nois"i*ly (?), adv. In a noisy manner.

noisiness.c: Noisiness Nois"i*ness, n. The state or quality of being noisy.

noisome.c: Noisome Noi"some (?), a. [For noysome, fr. noy for annoy. See Annoy.] 1. Noxious to health; hurtful; mischievous; unwholesome; insalubrious; destructive; as, noisome effluvia. “Noisome pestilence.” Ps. xci. 3.

noisy.c: Noisy Nois"y (?), a. [Compar. Noisier (?); superl. Noisiest.] [From Noise.] 1. Making a noise, esp. a loud sound; clamorous; vociferous; turbulent; boisterous; as, the noisy crowd.

nolde.c: Nolde Nol"de (?). [Contr. fr. ne wolde.] Would not. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nole.c: Nole Nole (?), n. [See Noll.] The head. [Obs.] Shak.

nolimetangere.c: Noli-me-tangere ‖No"li-me-tan"ge*re (?), n. [L., touch me not.] 1. (Bot.) (a) Any plant of a genus of herbs (Impatiens) having capsules which, if touched when ripe, discharge their seeds. -- See Impatiens. (b) The squirting cucumber. See under Cucumber.

nolition.c: Nolition No*li"tion (?), n. [L. nolle not to will, to be unwilling; ne + velle to will, to be willing.] Adverse action of will; unwillingness; -- opposed to volition.

noll.c: Noll Noll (?), n. [OE. nol, AS. hnoll top; akin to OHG. hnol top, head.] The head; the noodle. [Obs.]

nolleity.c: Nolleity Nol*le"i*ty (?), n. [L. nolle to be unwilling.] The state of being unwilling; nolition. [R.]

nolle.c: Nolle prosequi ‖Nol"le pros"e*qui (?). [L., to be unwilling to prosecute.] (Law) Will not prosecute; -- an entry on the record, denoting that a plaintiff discontinues his suit, or the attorney for the public a prosecution; either wholly, or as to some count, or as to some of several defendants.

nolo.c: Nolo contendere ‖No"lo con*ten"de*re (?). [L., I do not wish to contend.] (Law) A plea, by the defendant, in a criminal prosecution, which, without admitting guilt, subjects him to all the consequences of a plea of guilty.

nol.c: Nol pros. Nol. pros. An abbrev. of Nolle prosequi.

nolpros.c: Nol-pros Nol`-pros" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. -prossed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. -prossing.] To discontinue by entering a nolle prosequi; to decline to prosecute.

nolt.c: Nolt Nolt (?), n. sing. & pl. Neat cattle. [Prov. Eng.]

noma.c: Noma ‖No"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, lit., a feeding. See Name.] (Med.) See Canker, n., 1.

nomad.c: Nomad Nom"ad (?), n. [L. nomas, -adis, Gr.?,?, pasturing, roaming without fixed home, fr.? a pasture, allotted abode, fr.? to distribute, allot, drive to pasture; prob. akin to AS. niman to take, and E. nimble: cf. F. nomade. Cf. Astronomy, Economy, Nimble, Nemesis, Numb, Number.] One of a race or tribe that has no fixed location, but wanders from place to place in search of pasture or game.

nomadic.c: Nomadic No*mad"ic (?), a. [Gr.?. See Nomad.] Of or pertaining to nomads, or their way of life; wandering; moving from place to place for subsistence; as, a nomadic tribe. -- No*mad"ic*al*ly (#), adv.

nomadism.c: Nomadism Nom"ad*ism (?), n. The state of being a nomad.

nomadize.c: Nomadize Nom"ad*ize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Nomadized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nomadizing (?).] To lead the life of a nomad; to wander with flocks and herds for the sake of finding pasturage.

nomancy.c: Nomancy No"man*cy (?), n. [Cf. F. nomancie, nomance, abbrev. fr. onomancie. See Onomancy.] The art or practice of divining the destiny of persons by the letters which form their names.

nomansland.c: No-man's-land No-man's land No"-man's` land`, No"-man's`-land` (?). 1. (Naut.) A space amidships used to keep blocks, ropes, etc.; a space on a ship belonging to no one in particular to care for.

nomarch.c: Nomarch Nom"arch (?), n. [Gr.? a district + -arch.] The chief magistrate of a nome or nomarchy.

nomarchy.c: Nomarchy Nom"arch*y (?), n.; pl. Nomarchies (?). A province or territorial division of a kingdom, under the rule of a nomarch, as in modern Greece; a nome.

nombles.c: Nombles Nom"bles (?), n. pl. [F. nombles, fr. L. lumbulus, dim. of lumbus a loin. Cf. Numbles, Umbles, Humbles.] The entrails of a deer; the umbles. [Written also numbles.] Johnson.

nombril.c: Nombril Nom"bril (?), n. [F. nombril, for OF. lombril, i. e., ombril, with the article, a dim. fr. L. umbilicus the navel. See Navel.] (Her.) A point halfway between the fess point and the middle base point of an escutcheon; -- called also navel point. See Escutcheon.

nome.c: Nome Nome (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? to deal out, distribute.] 1. A province or political division, as of modern Greece or ancient Egypt; a nomarchy.

nomen.c: Nomen Nome { Nome, No"men (?) }, obs. p. p. of Nim. Chaucer.

nomenclator.c: Nomenclator No"men*cla`tor (?), n. [L., fr. nomen name + calare to call. See Name, and Calendar.] 1. One who calls persons or things by their names.

nomenclatural.c: Nomenclatural No`men*cla"tur*al (?), a. Pertaining or according to a nomenclature.

nomenclature.c: Nomenclature No"men*cla`ture (?), n. [L. nomenclatura: cf. F. nomenclature. See Nomenclator.] 1. A name. [Obs.] Bacon.

nomial.c: Nomial No"mi*al (?), n. [Cf. Binomial.] (Alg.) A name or term.

nomic.c: Nomic Nom"ic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? a law, custom.] Customary; ordinary; -- applied to the usual English spelling, in distinction from strictly phonetic methods. H Sweet. -- n. Nomic spelling. A. J. Ellis.

nominal.c: Nominal Nom"i*nal (?), a. [L. nominalis, fr. nomen, nominis, name. See Name.] 1. Of or pertaining to a name or names; having to do with the literal meaning of a word; verbal; as, a nominal definition. Bp. Pearson.

nominalism.c: Nominalism Nom"i*nal*ism (?), n. The principles or philosophy of the Nominalists.

nominalist.c: Nominalist Nom"i*nal*ist, n. (Metaph.) One of a sect of philosophers in the Middle Ages, who adopted the opinion of Roscelin, that general conceptions, or universals, exist in name only. Reid.

nominalistic.c: Nominalistic Nom`i*nal*is"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Nominalists.

nominalize.c: Nominalize Nom"i*nal*ize (?), v. t. (Grammar, Linguistics) To convert into a noun; as, a nominalized sentence; a nominalized adjective or verb.

nominally.c: Nominally Nom"i*nal*ly, adv. In a nominal manner; by name; in name only; not in reality. Burke.

nominate.c: Nominate Nom"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nominated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nominating (?).] [L. nominatus, p. p. of nominare to nominate, fr. nomen name. See Name.]

nominately.c: Nominately Nom"i*nate*ly (?), adv. By name; particularly; namely. [Obs.] Spelman.

nomination.c: Nomination Nom`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. nominatio: cf. F. nomination.]

nominatival.c: Nominatival Nom`i*na*ti"val (?), a. (Gram.) Of or pertaining to the nominative case.

nominative.c: Nominative Nom"i*na*tive (?), a. [L. nominativus belonging to a name, nominative.] (Gram.) Giving a name; naming; designating; -- said of that case or form of a noun which stands as the subject of a finite verb. -- n. The nominative case.

nominatively.c: Nominatively Nom"i*na*tive*ly, adv. In the manner of a nominative; as a nominative.

nominee.c: Nominee Nom`i*nee" (?), n. [See Nominate, and -ee.] A person named, or designated, by another, to any office, duty, or position; one nominated, or proposed, by others for office or for election to office. One remains a nominee until one has been elected or has assumed the office.

nominor.c: Nominor Nom"i*nor` (?), n. [See Nominate, and -or.] A nominator. [Obs.] Bentham.

nomocracy.c: Nomocracy No*moc"ra*cy (?), n. [Gr. no`mos law + -cracy, as in democracy.] Government in accordance with a system of law. Milman.

nomography.c: Nomography No*mog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.?; no`mos law +? to write.] A treatise on laws; an exposition of the form proper for laws.

nomopelmous.c: Nomopelmous Nom`o*pel"mous (?), a. [Gr. no`mos law, custom +? sole of the foot.] (Zool.) Having a separate and simple tendon to flex the first toe, or hallux, as do passerine birds.

nomothete.c: Nomothete Nom"o*thete (?), n. [Gr.?; no`mos +? to assign: cf. F. nomothète.] A lawgiver. [R.]

nomothetical.c: Nomothetical Nomothetic { Nom`o*thet"ic (?), Nom`o*thet"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?.] Legislative; enacting laws; as, a nomothetical power. [R.] Bp. Barlow.

non.c: Non Non (nŏn), a. No; not. See No, a. Chaucer.

Non- Non- (nŏn-) pref. [L. non, OL. noenu, noenum, fr. neoenum, lit., not one. See None.] A prefix used in the sense of not; un-; in-; as in nonattention, or non-attention, nonconformity, nonmetallic, nonsuit.
Non assumpsit ‖Non` as*sump"sit (?). [L., he did not undertake.] (Law) The general plea or denial in an action of assumpsit.

Non compos mentis Non compos { ‖Non com"pos (?). ‖Non com"pos men"tis (?). } [L.] Not of sound mind; not having the regular use of reason; hence, also, as a noun, an idiot; a lunatic; one devoid of reason, either by nature or from accident.
Non est factum ‖Non` est` fac"tum (?). [Law L. it is not (his) deed.] (Law) The plea of the general issue in an action of debt on bond.
Non est inventus ‖Non` est` in*ven"tus (?). [L., he is not found.] (Law) The return of a sheriff on a writ, when the defendant is not found in his county. Bouvier.
Non liquet ‖Non` li"quet (?). [L.] It is not clear; -- a verdict given by a jury when a matter is to be deferred to another day of trial.
Non obstante ‖Non` ob*stan"te (nŏn` ŏb*stăn"te). [L.] 1. Notwithstanding; in opposition to, or in spite of, what has been stated, or is to be stated or admitted.
Non pros. Non" pros.` (?). An abbreviation of Non prosequitur.
Non prosequitur ‖Non" pro*seq"ui*tur (?). [L. he does not prosecute.] (Law) A judgment entered against the plaintiff in a suit where he does not appear to prosecute. See Nolle prosequi.
Non sequitur ‖Non seq"ui*tur (?). [L., it does not follow.] (Logic) An inference which does not follow from the premises.

nonacceptance.c: Nonacceptance Non`ac*cept"ance (?), n. A neglect or refusal to accept.

nonacid.c: Nonacid Non*ac"id (nŏn*ăs"ĭd), a. (Chem.) Destitute of acid properties; hence, basic; metallic; positive; -- said of certain atoms and radicals.

nonacquaintance.c: Nonacquaintance Non`ac*quaint"ance (?), n. Want of acquaintance; the state of being unacquainted.

nonacquiescence.c: Nonacquiescence Non*ac`qui*es"cence (?), n. Refusal of acquiescence; failure to yield or comply.

nonadmission.c: Nonadmission Non`ad*mis"sion (?), n. Failure to be admitted.

nonaerobiotic.c: Nonaerobiotic Non*a`er*o*bi*ot"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Capable of living without atmospheric oxygen; anaerobic.

nonage.c: Nonage Non"age (?), n. [LL. nonagium, from L. nonus ninth, novem nine.] (Eccl.) The ninth part of movable goods, formerly payable to the clergy on the death of persons in their parishes. Mozley & W.
Nonage Non"age, n. [Pref. non- + age.] Time of life before a person becomes of age; legal immaturity; minority.

nonaged.c: Nonaged Non"aged (?), a. Having the quality of nonage; being a minor; immature. W. Browne.

nonagenarian.c: Nonagenarian Non`a*ge*na"ri*an (?), n. [L. nonagenarius containing, or consisting of, ninety, fr. nonageni ninety each; akin to novem nine.] A person ninety years old.

nonagesimal.c: Nonagesimal Non`a*ges"i*mal (?), a. [L. nonagesimus the ninetieth. See Nonagenarian.] (Astron.) Of or pertaining to the ninetieth degree or to a nonagesimal.

Nonagesimal Non`a*ges"i*mal, n. (Astron.) The middle or highest point of the part of the ecliptic which is at any given moment above the horizon. It is the ninetieth degree of the ecliptic, reckoned from the points in which it is intersected by the horizon.

nonagon.c: Nonagon Non"a*gon (?), n. [L. nonus ninth + Gr.? angle.] (Math.) A plane figure or polygon having nine sides and nine angles.

nonagrian.c: Nonagrian Non*a"gri*an (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) Any moth of the genus Nonagria and allied genera, as the spindleworm and stalk borer.

nonalienation.c: Nonalienation Non*al`ien*a"tion (?), n. Failure to alienate; also, the state of not being alienated.

nonane.c: Nonane Non"ane (?), n. [L. nonus ninth.] (Chem.) One of a group of metameric hydrocarbons C9H20 of the paraffin series; -- so called because of the nine carbon atoms in the molecule. Normal nonane is a colorless volatile liquid, an ingredient of ordinary kerosene.

nonappearance.c: Nonappearance Non`ap*pear"ance (?), n. Default of appearance, as in court, to prosecute or defend; failure to appear.

nonappointment.c: Nonappointment Non`ap*point"ment (?), n. Neglect of making appointment; failure to receive an appointment.

nonattendance.c: Nonattendance Non`at*tend"ance (?), n. A failure to attend; omission of attendance; nonappearance.

nonbituminous.c: Nonbituminous Non`bi*tu"mi*nous (?), a. Containing no bitumen; not bituminous.

nonce.c: Nonce Nonce (nŏns), n. [For the nonce, OE. for the nones, a corruption of for then ones, where n. in then is a relic of AS. m in ðam, dat. of the article and demonstrative pronoun, E. the. See For, Once, and The.] The one or single occasion; the present call or purpose; -- chiefly used in the phrase for the nonce, i. e. for the present time.

nonchalance.c: Nonchalance ‖Non`cha`lance" (?), n. [F. See Nonchalant.] Indifference; carelessness; coolness.

nonchalant.c: Nonchalant ‖Non`cha`lant" (?), a. [F., fr. non not (L. non) + chaloir to concern one's self for, fr. L. calere to be warm, to be inflamed with desire, to be troubled. See Non-, and Caldron.] Indifferent; careless; cool.

nonchalantly.c: Nonchalantly Non"cha*lant`ly (?), adv. In a nonchalant, indifferent, or careless manner; coolly.

nonclaim.c: Nonclaim Non"claim` (?), n. A failure to make claim within the time limited by law; omission of claim.

noncombatant.c: Noncombatant Non*com"bat*ant (?), n. 1. (Mil.) Any person connected with an army, or within the lines of an army, who does not make it his business to fight, as any one of the medical officers and their assistants, chaplains, and others; also, any of the citizens of a place occupied by an army; also, any one holding a similar position with respect to the navy.

noncommissioned.c: Noncommissioned Non`com*mis"sioned (?), a. Not having a commission.

noncommittal.c: Noncommittal Non`com*mit"tal (?), n. A state of not being committed or pledged; forbearance or refusal to commit one's self. Also used adjectively.

noncommunion.c: Noncommunion Non`com*mun"ion (?), n. Neglect or failure of communion.

noncompletion.c: Noncompletion Non`com*ple"tion (?), n. Lack of completion; failure to complete.

noncompliance.c: Noncompliance Non`com*pli"ance (?), n. Neglect of compliance; failure to comply.

noncomplying.c: Noncomplying Non`com*ply"ing (?), a. Neglecting or refusing to comply.

nonconcur.c: Nonconcur Non`con*cur" (?), v. i. To dissent or refuse to concur.

noncondensible.c: Noncondensible Non`con*den"si*ble (?), a. Not condensible; incapable of being liquefied; -- said of gases. [archaic]

noncondensing.c: Noncondensing Non`con*dens"ing, a. (Steam Engine) Not condensing; discharging the steam from the cylinder at a pressure nearly equal to or above that of the atmosphere and not into a condenser.

nonconducting.c: Nonconducting Non`con*duct"ing (?), a. Not conducting; nonconductive; not transmitting a fluid or force; -- used especially of electric current; thus, in electricity, wax is a nonconducting substance.

nonconduction.c: Nonconduction Non`con*duc"tion (?), n. The quality of not being able to conduct or transmit; failure to conduct.

nonconductor.c: Nonconductor Non`con*duct"or (?), n. (Physics) A substance which does not conduct, that is, convey or transmit, heat, electricity, sound, vibration, or the like, or which transmits them with difficulty; an insulator; as, wool is a nonconductor of heat; glass and dry wood are nonconductors of electricity.

nonconforming.c: Nonconforming Non`con*form"ing (?), a. Not conforming; declining conformity; especially, not conforming to the established church of a country.

nonconformist.c: Nonconformist Non`con*form"ist, n. One who does not conform to an established church; especially, one who does not conform to the established church of England; a dissenter.

nonconformity.c: Nonconformity Non*con*form"i*ty (?), n. Neglect or failure of conformity; especially, in England, the neglect or refusal to unite with the established church in its rites and modes of worship.

nonconstat.c: Nonconstat ‖Non`con"stat (?), n. [Law L.] It does not appear; it is not plain or clear; it does not follow.

noncontagious.c: Noncontagious Non`con*ta"gious (?), a. Not contagious; not catching; not communicable by contact. -- Non`con*ta"gious*ness, n.

noncontent.c: Noncontent Non`con*tent" (?), n. (British House of Lords) One who gives a negative vote; -- sometimes abridged into noncon. or non con.

noncontributory.c: Noncontributory Noncontributing { Non`con*trib"u*ting (?), Non`con*trib"u*to*ry (?) }, a. Not contributing.

nonda.c: Nonda Non"da (?), n. (Bot.) The edible plumlike fruit of the Australian tree, Parinarium Nonda.

nondecane.c: Nondecane Non*dec"ane (?), n. [L. nonus ninth + decem ten.] (Chem.) A hydrocarbon of the paraffin series, a white waxy substance, C19H40; -- so called from the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

nondeciduate.c: Nondeciduate Non`de*cid"u*ate (?), a. (Anat.) Characterized by the absence of a decidua; indeciduate.

nondelivery.c: Nondelivery Non`de*liv"er*y (?), n. A neglect or failure of delivery; omission of delivery.

nondeposition.c: Nondeposition Non*dep`o*si"tion (?), n. A failure to deposit or throw down.

nondescript.c: nondescript non"de*script (?), a. [Pref. non- + L. descriptus described.] 1. Not hitherto described; hence, of no recognizable type or class; odd; abnormal; unclassifiable.
Nondescript Non"de*script, n. A thing not yet described; that of which no account or explanation has been given; something abnormal, or hardly classifiable.

nondevelopment.c: Nondevelopment Non`de*vel"op*ment (?), n. Failure or lack of development.

nondiscovery.c: Nondiscovery Non`dis*cov"er*y (?), n. Want or failure of discovery.

nondo.c: Nondo Non"do (?), n. (Bot.) A coarse umbelliferous plant (Ligusticum actaeifolium) with a large aromatic root. It is found chiefly in the Alleghany region. Also called Angelico.

none.c: None None (nŭn), a. & pron. [OE. none, non, nan, no, na, AS. nān, fr. ne not + ān one. √193. See No, a. & adv., One, and cf. Non-, Null, a.]

nonego.c: Non-ego ‖Non-e"go (?), n. [L., not I.] (Metaph.) The union of being and relation as distinguished from, and contrasted with, the ego. See Ego.

nonelastic.c: Nonelastic Non`e*las"tic (?), a. Not having elasticity; not able to be stretched reversibly.

nonelect.c: Nonelect Non`e*lect" (?), n. sing. & pl. (Theol.) A person or persons not elected, or chosen, to salvation.

nonelectrical.c: Nonelectrical Nonelectric { Non`e*lec"tric (?), Non`e*lec"tric*al (?) }, a. 1. Not electric; conducting electricity. [archaic]

nonelectric.c: Nonelectric Non`e*lec"tric, n. (Physics) A substance that is not an insulator (i. e., an electric); that which transmits electricity, as a metal; a conductor. [archaic]

nonemphatical.c: Nonemphatical Nonemphatic { Non`em*phat"ic (?), Non`em*phat"ic*al (?) }, a. Having no emphasis; unemphatic.

nonentity.c: Nonentity Non*en"ti*ty (?), n.; pl. Nonentities (?). 1. Nonexistence; the negation of being.

nonepiscopal.c: Non-Episcopal Non`-E*pis"co*pal (?), a. Not Episcopal; not pertaining to the Episcopal church or system.

nones.c: Nones Nones (?), n. pl. [L. nonae, so called because it was the ninth day before the ides, fr. nonus ninth, from novem nine. See Nine, Nones, 2, Noon.]

nonessential.c: Nonessential Non`es*sen"tial, n. A thing not essential.

nonesuch.c: Nonesuch None"such` (?), n. A person or thing of a sort that there is no other such; something extraordinary; a thing that has not its equal. It is given as a name to various objects, as to a choice variety of apple, a species of medic (Medicago lupulina), a variety of pottery clay, etc.

nonetto.c: Nonetto Nonet { No*net" (?), ‖No*net"to (?) }, n. [From L. nonus ninth, like E. duet, fr. L. duo.] (Mus.) A composition for nine instruments, rarely for nine voices.

nonexecution.c: Nonexecution Non*ex`e*cu"tion (?), n. Neglect or failure of execution; nonperformance.

nonexistence.c: Nonexistence Non`ex*ist"ence (?), n. 1. The state of not existing; absence of existence; the negation of being; -- usually used with reference to existince in the real world, or logical possiblity; as, the nonexistence of vaporware does not go unnoticed long. A. Baxter.

nonexportation.c: Nonexportation Non*ex`por*ta"tion (?), n. A failure of exportation; a not exporting of commodities.

nonextensile.c: Nonextensile Non`ex*ten"sile (?), a. Not extensile; incapable of being stretched.

nonfeasance.c: Non-feasance Non-fea"sance (?), n. [Pref. non- + OF. faisance a doing, fr. faire to do.] (Law) An omission or neglect to do something, esp. that which ought to have been done. Cf. Malfeasance.

nonfulfillment.c: Nonfulfillment Non`ful*fill"ment, n. Neglect or failure to fulfill.

nonillion.c: Nonillion No*nil"lion (?), n. [L. nonus ninth + -illion, as in E. million.] According to the French and American notation, a thousand octillions, or a unit with thirty ciphers annexed; according to the English notation, a million octillions, or a unit with fifty-four ciphers annexed. See the Note under Numeration.

nonimportation.c: Nonimportation Non*im`por*ta"tion (?), n. Want or failure of importation; a not importing of commodities.

nonimporting.c: Nonimporting Non`im*port"ing (?), a. Not importing; not bringing from foreign countries.

noninflectional.c: Noninflectional Non`in*flec"tion*al (?), a. Not admitting of, or characterized by, inflection.

noninhabitant.c: Noninhabitant Non`in*hab"it*ant (?), n. One who is not an inhabitant; a stranger; a foreigner; a nonresident.

nonintervention.c: Nonintervention Non*in`ter*ven"tion (?), n. The state or habit of not intervening or interfering; as, the nonintervention of one state in the affairs of another.

nonius.c: Nonius No"ni*us (?), n. [Latinized form of Nunez, the name of a Portuguese mathematician.] A vernier.

nonjoinder.c: Nonjoinder Non*join"der (?), n. (Law) The omission of some person who ought to have been made a plaintiff or defendant in a suit, or of some cause of action which ought to be joined.

nonjuring.c: Nonjuring Non*ju"ring (?), a. [F. jurer to swear, or L. jurare, jurari, to swear, fr. L. jus, juris, right, law, justice. See Jury.] Not swearing allegiance; -- applied to the party in Great Britain that would not swear allegiance to William and Mary, or their successors.

nonjuror.c: Nonjuror Non*ju"ror (?), n. (Eng. Hist.) One of those adherents of James II. who refused to take the oath of allegiance to William and Mary, or to their successors, after the revolution of 1688; a Jacobite.

nonjurorism.c: Nonjurorism Non*ju"ror*ism (?), n. (Eng. Hist.) The doctrines, or action, of the Nonjurors.

nonlimitation.c: Nonlimitation Non*lim`i*ta"tion (?), n. Want of limitation; failure to limit.

nonmalignant.c: Nonmalignant Non`ma*lig"nant (?), a. Not malignant, as a disease; -- used especially of tumors; as, a nonmalignant growth on the liver.

nonmanufacturing.c: Nonmanufacturing Non*man`u*fac"tur*ing (?), a. Not carrying on manufactures.

nonmedullated.c: Nonmedullated Non*med"ul*la`ted (?), a. Not medullated; Specifically: (Anat.) without a medulla or marrow, or without a medullary sheath; as, a nonmedullated nerve fiber.

nonmember.c: Nonmember Non*mem"ber, n. One who is not a member; as, nonmembers are not allowed in the club reading room.

nonmembership.c: Nonmembership Non*mem"ber*ship, n. State of not being a member.

nonmetal.c: Nonmetal Non"met`al (?), n. (Chem.) Any one of the set of elements which, as contrasted with the metals, possess, produce, or receive, acid rather than basic properties; a metalloid; as, oxygen, sulphur, and chlorine are nonmetals.

nonmoral.c: Nonmoral Non*mor"al (?), a. Neither moral nor immoral; having no connection with morals; not within the sphere of morals or ethics; not ethical; as, imagination is of its nature nonmoral; infants are nonmoral.

nonnecessity.c: Nonnecessity Non`ne*ces"si*ty (?), n. Absence of necessity; the quality or state of being unnecessary.

nonnitrogenous.c: Nonnitrogenous Non`ni*trog"e*nous (?), a. Devoid of nitrogen; as, a nonnitrogenous principle; a nonnitrogenous food. See the Note under Food, n., 1.

nonnucleated.c: Nonnucleated Non*nu"cle*a`ted (?), a. Without a nucleus; anucleate.

nonny.c: Nonny Non"ny (?), n. A silly fellow; a ninny.

nonobedience.c: Nonobedience Non`o*be"di*ence (nŏn`o*bē"dĭ*eins), n. Neglect of obedience; failure to obey.

nonobservance.c: Nonobservance Non`ob*serv"ance (nŏn`ŏb*zẽrv"ains), n. Neglect or failure to observe or fulfill.

nonoic.c: Nonoic No*no"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, nonane; as, nonoic acid, which is also called pelargonic acid. Cf. Pelargonic.

nonone.c: Nonone Non"one (?), n. [Nonane + -one, suffix denoting the third degree of unsaturation.] (Chem.) 1. Any one of several metameric unsaturated hydrocarbons (C9H14) of the valylene series. [archaic?]

nonoxygenous.c: Nonoxygenous Non`ox*yg"e*nous (?), a. (Chem.) Without oxygen; characterized by the absence of oxygen; as, a nonoxygenous alkaloid.

nonpareil.c: Nonpareil Non`pa*reil" (?), n. [See Nonpareil, a. ] 1. Something of unequaled excellence; a peerless thing or person; a nonesuch; -- often used as a name.
Nonpareil Non`pa*reil", a. [F., from non not + pareil equal, fr. LL. pariculus, dim. of L. par equal. See Non, and Pair, Peer.] Having no equal; peerless.

nonpayment.c: Nonpayment Non*pay"ment, n. Neglect or failure to pay.

nonperformance.c: Nonperformance Non`per*form"ance, n. Neglect or failure to perform.

nonphotobiotic.c: Nonphotobiotic Non*pho`to*bi*ot"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Capable of living without light; as, nonphotobiotic plant cells, or cells which habitually live in darkness.

nonplane.c: Nonplane Non`plane" (?), a. (Math.) Not lying in one plane; not planar; -- said of certain curves.

nonplus.c: Nonplus Non"plus (?), n. [L. non not + plus more, further. See Plural.] A state or condition which baffles reason or confounds judgment; insuperable difficulty; inability to proceed or decide; puzzle; quandary.
Nonplus Non"plus` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nonplused (?) or Nonplussed; p. pr. & vb. n. Nonplusing or Nonplussing.] To puzzle; to confound; to perplex; to cause to stop by embarrassment.

nonpreparation.c: Nonpreparation Non*prep`a*ra"tion (?), n. Neglect or failure to prepare; want of preparation.

nonpresentation.c: Nonpresentation Non*pres`en*ta"tion (?), n. Neglect or failure to present; state of not being presented.

nonproduction.c: Nonproduction Non`pro*duc"tion, n. A failure to produce or exhibit.

nonprofessional.c: Nonprofessional Non`pro*fes"sion*al (?), a. 1. Not belonging to a profession.

nonproficiency.c: Nonproficiency Non`pro*fi"cien*cy (?), n. Want of proficiency; failure to make progress.

nonproficient.c: Nonproficient Non`pro*fi"cient (?), n. One who has failed to become proficient.

nonpros.c: Non-pros Non`-pros" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nonprossed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Non-prossing (?).] To decline or fail to prosecute; to allow to be dropped (said of a suit); to enter judgment against (a plaintiff who fails to prosecute); as, the plaintiff was non-prossed.

nonrecurring.c: Nonrecurring Non`re*cur"ring (?), a. Nonrecurrent; as, the costs of a layoff are considered as a nonrecurring expense.

nonregardance.c: Nonregardance Non`re*gard"ance (?), n. Want of due regard; disregard; slight. [Obs.] Shak.

nonregent.c: Nonregent Non`re"gent (?), n. (Eng. Universities) A master of arts whose regency has ceased. See Regent.

nonrendition.c: Nonrendition Non`ren*di"tion (?), n. Neglect of rendition; the not rendering what is due.

nonresemblance.c: Nonresemblance Non`re*sem"blance (?), n. Want of resemblance; unlikeness; dissimilarity.

nonresidence.c: Nonresidence Non*res"i*dence (?), n. The state or condition of being nonresident, Swift.

nonresident.c: Nonresident Non*res"i*dent (?), a. Not residing in a particular place, on one's own estate, or in one's proper place; as, a nonresident clergyman or proprietor of lands.
Nonresident Non*res"i*dent, n. A nonresident person; one who does not reside in the State or jurisdiction.

nonresistance.c: Nonresistance Non`re*sist"ance (?), n. The principles or practice of a nonresistant; passive obedience; submission to authority, power, oppression, or violence without opposition.

nonresistant.c: Nonresistant Non`re*sist"ant, n. 1. One who maintains that no resistance should be made to constituted authority, even when unjustly or oppressively exercised; one who advocates or practices absolute submission.

nonruminant.c: Nonruminant Non*ru"mi*nant (?), a. Not ruminating; as, a nonruminant animal.

nonsane.c: Nonsane Non`sane" (?), a. Unsound; not perfect; as, a person of nonsane memory. Blackstone.

nonsense.c: Nonsense Non"sense (?), n. [Pref. non- + sense: cf. F. nonsens.] 1. That which is not sense, or has no sense; words, or language, which have no meaning, or which convey no intelligible ideas; absurdity.

nonsensical.c: Nonsensical Non*sen"si*cal (?), a. Without sense; unmeaning; absurd; foolish; irrational; preposterous. -- Non*sen"si*cal*ly, adv. -- Non*sen"si*cal*ness, n.

nonsensitive.c: Nonsensitive Non*sen"si*tive (?), a. Not sensitive; wanting sense or perception; not easily affected.

nonsexual.c: Nonsexual Non*sex"u*al (?), a. Having no distinction of sex; sexless; neuter.

nonslaveholding.c: Nonslaveholding Non*slave"hold`ing (?), a. Not possessing or holding slaves; as, a nonslaveholding State.

nonsolution.c: Nonsolution Non`so*lu"tion (?), n. Failure of solution or explanation.

nonsolvency.c: Nonsolvency Non*sol"ven*cy (?), n. Inability to pay debts; insolvency.

nonsonant.c: Nonsonant Non*so"nant (?), a. Not sonant. -- n. A nonsonant or nonvocal consonant.

nonstriated.c: Nonstriated Non*stri"a*ted (?), a. (Nat. Hist.) Without striations; unstriped; as, nonstriated muscle fibers.

nonsubmission.c: Nonsubmission Non`sub*mis"sion (?), n. Want of submission; failure or refusal to submit.

nonsuit.c: Nonsuit Non"suit` (?), n. (Law) A neglect or failure by the plaintiff to follow up his suit; a stopping of the suit; a renunciation or withdrawal of the cause by the plaintiff, either because he is satisfied that he can not support it, or upon the judge's expressing his opinion. A compulsory nonsuit is a nonsuit ordered by the court on the ground that the plaintiff on his own showing has not made out his case.

Nonsuit Non"suit`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nonsuited; p. pr. & vb. n. Nonsuiting.] (Law) To determine, adjudge, or record (a plaintiff) as having dropped his suit, upon his withdrawal or failure to follow it up. “When two are joined in a writ, and one is nonsuited.” Z. Swift.
Nonsuit Non"suit`, a. Nonsuited. D. A. Tyng.

nontenure.c: Nontenure Non*ten"ure (?), n. (Law) A plea of a defendant that he did not hold the land, as affirmed.

nonterm.c: Nonterm Non"term` (?), n. (Law) A vacation between two terms of a court.

nontronite.c: Nontronite Non"tro*nite (?), n. [So called because found in the arrondissement of Nontron, France.] (Min.) A greenish yellow or green mineral, consisting chiefly of the hydrous silicate of iron.

nonuniformist.c: Nonuniformist Non*u"ni*form`ist (?), n. One who believes that past changes in the structure of the earth have proceeded from cataclysms or causes more violent than are now operating; -- called also nonuniformitarian.

nonunion.c: Nonunion Non*un"ion (?), a. 1. Not belonging to, or affiliated with, a trades union; as, a nonunion carpenter.

nonunionist.c: Nonunionist Non*un"ion*ist (?), n. One who does not belong, or refuses to belong, to a trades union.

nonusance.c: Nonusance Non*us"ance (?), n. Neglect of using; failure to use. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

nonuser.c: Nonuser Non*us"er (?), 1. A not using; failure to use.

nonvascular.c: Nonvascular Non*vas"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Destitute of vessels; extravascular.

nonvocal.c: Nonvocal Non*vo"cal (?), a. Not vocal; destitute of tone. -- n. A nonvocal consonant.

nonyl.c: Nonyl Non"yl (?), n. [Nonane + -yl.] (Chem.) The hydrocarbon radical, C9H19-, derived from nonane and forming many compounds. Used also adjectively; as, nonyl alcohol.

nonylene.c: Nonylene Non"y*lene (?), n. [Nonane + ethylene.] (Chem.) Any one of a series of metameric, unsaturated hydrocarbons C9H18 of the ethylene series.

nonylenic.c: Nonylenic Non`y*len"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, related to, or designating, nonylene or its compounds; as, nonylenic acid.

nonylic.c: Nonylic No*nyl"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, nonyl or its compounds; as, nonylic acid.

noodle.c: Noodle Noo"dle (?), n. [Cf. Noddle, Noddy.] 1. A simpleton; a blockhead; a stupid person; a ninny. [Low]
Noodle Noo"dle, n. [G. nudel vermicelli.] A thin strip of dough, made with eggs, rolled up, cut into small pieces, and used in soup.

nook.c: Nook Nook (nŏok; 277), n. [OE. nok; cf. Gael. & Ir. niuc.] A narrow place formed by an angle in bodies or between bodies; a corner; a recess; a secluded retreat.

nookshotten.c: Nook-shotten Nook"-shot`ten (?), a. Full of nooks, angles, or corners. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

noological.c: Noological No`o*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to noology.

noologist.c: Noologist No*ol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in no0logy.

noology.c: Noology No*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.?,?, the mind + -logy.] The science of intellectual phenomena.

noon.c: Noon Noon (nōn), a. No. See the Note under No. [Obs.]

Noon Noon (nōon), n. [AS. nōn, orig., the ninth hour, fr. L. nona (sc. hora) the ninth hour, then applied to the church services (called nones) at that hour, the time of which was afterwards changed to noon. See Nine, and cf. Nones, Nunchion.] 1. The middle of the day; midday; the time when the sun is in the meridian; twelve o'clock in the daytime.
Noon Noon (?), a. Belonging to midday; occurring at midday; meridional. Young.
Noon Noon, v. i. To take rest and refreshment at noon.

noonday.c: Noonday Noon"day` (?), n. Midday; twelve o'clock in the day; noon.
Noonday Noon"day` (?), a. Of or pertaining to midday; meridional; as, the noonday heat; only mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the noonday sun. “Noonday walks.” Addison.

noonflower.c: Noon-flower Noon"-flow`er (?), n. (Bot.) The goat's beard, whose flowers close at midday.

nooning.c: Nooning Noon"ing, n. A rest at noon; a repast at noon.

noonstead.c: Noonstead Noon"stead (?), n. The position of the sun at noon. [Obs.] Drayton.

noontide.c: Noontide Noon"tide` (?), n. [From noon + tide time; cf. AS. nōntīd the ninth hour.] The time of noon; midday.

noose.c: Noose Noose (?), n. [Prob. fr. OF. nous, nom. sing. or acc. pl. of nou knot, F. nœud, L. nodus. Cf. Node.] A running knot, or loop, which binds the closer the more it is drawn.
Noose Noose (nōoz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Noosed (nōozd); p. pr. & vb. n. Noosing.] To tie in a noose; to catch in a noose; to entrap; to insnare.

nopal.c: Nopal No"pal (?), n. [Mexican nopalli.] (Bot.) A cactaceous plant (Nopalea cochinellifera), originally Mexican, on which the cochineal insect feeds, and from which it is collected. The name is sometimes given to other species of Cactaceae.

nopalry.c: Nopalry No"pal*ry (?), n.; pl. Nopalries (?). A plantation of the nopal for raising the cochineal insect.

nor.c: Nor Nor (nôr), conj. [OE. nor, contr. from nother. See Neither.] A negative connective or particle, introducing the second member or clause of a negative proposition, following neither, or not, in the first member or clause (as or in affirmative propositions follows either). Nor is also used sometimes in the first member for neither, and sometimes the neither is omitted and implied by the use of nor.

norfolk.c: Norfolk Nor"folk (?), n. Short for Norfolk Jacket.
Norfolk dumpling Norfolk dumpling. (Eng.) (a) A kind of boiled dumpling made in Norfolk. (b) A native or inhabitant of Norfolk.
Norfolk jacket Norfolk jacket. A kind of loose-fitting plaited jacket, having a loose belt.
Norfolk plover Norfolk plover. The stone curlew.
Norfolk spaniel Norfolk spaniel. One of a breed of field spaniels similar to the clumbers, but shorter in body and of a liver-and-white or black-and-white color.

noria.c: Noria No"ri*a (nō"rĭ*ȧ), n. [Sp., from Ar. nā'ūra.] A large water wheel, turned by the action of a stream against its floats, and carrying at its circumference buckets, by which water is raised and discharged into a trough; used in Arabia, China, and elsewhere for irrigating land; a Persian wheel.

norian.c: Norian No"ri*an (?), a. [From norite.] (Geol.) Pertaining to the upper portion of the Laurentian rocks. T. S. Hunt.

norie.c: Norie No"rie (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) The cormorant. [Prov. Eng.]

norimon.c: Norimon Nor"i*mon (?), n.; pl. Norimons (?). A Japanese covered litter, carried by men. B. Taylor.
