norite.c: Norite No"rite (?), n. [F., fr. Norvège Norway.] (Min.) A granular crystalline rock consisting essentially of a triclinic feldspar (as labradorite) and hypersthene.

norium.c: norium no"ri*um (?), n. [NL.] (Chem.) A supposed metal alleged to have been discovered in 1845 by the Swedish chemist Swanberg in zircon. After many unsuccessful attempts to verify this new element, the element named Hafnium (atomic number 72) was discoverd in 1923 by D. Coster and G. von Hevesey in the zirconium-containing mineral zircon. Hafnium, present at 1 to 5% in many zirconium-bearing minerals, but difficult to separate from zirconium, is probably the element that gave rise to the properties attributed to the hypothetical norium.

norland.c: Norland Nor"land (?), n. [For Northland.] 1. The land in the north; north country. [Chiefly Poetic]

norlander.c: Norlander Nor"land*er, n. A northener; a person from the north country.

norm.c: Norm Norm (?), n. [L. norma a rule. See Normal, a.]

norma.c: Norma Nor"ma (?), n. [L.] 1. A norm; a principle or rule; a model; a standard. J. S. Mill.

normal.c: Normal Nor"mal (nôr"mail), a. [L. normalis, fr. norma rule, pattern, carpenter's square; prob. akin to noscere to know; cf. Gr. gnw`rimos well known, gnw`mwn gnomon, also, carpenter's square: cf. F. normal. See Known, and cf. Abnormal, Enormous.]
Normal Nor"mal (nôr"mail), n. [Cf. F. normale, ligne normale. See Normal, a.] 1. (Geom.) Any perpendicular.

normalcy.c: normalcy nor"mal*cy (?), n. The quality, state, or fact of being normal; the normal situation or condition; as, the point of normalcy. [R.]

normalization.c: Normalization Nor`mal*i*za"tion (?), n. Reduction to a standard or normal state.

normally.c: normally nor"mal*ly, adv. In a normal manner. Darwin.

norman.c: norman nor"man (?), n. [F. normand.] (Naut.) A wooden bar, or iron pin. W. C. Russell.
Norman Nor"man, prop. a. [F. normand, of Scand. origin. See Northman, and cf. Norse.] Of or pertaining to Normandy or to the Normans; as, the Norman language; the Norman conquest.

Norman Nor"man, prop. n. A native or inhabitant of Normandy; originally, one of the Northmen or Scandinavians who conquered Normandy in the 10th century; afterwards, one of the mixed (Norman-French) race which conquered England, under William the Conqueror.

normanism.c: Normanism Nor"man*ism (?), n. A Norman idiom; a custom or expression peculiar to the Normans. M. Arnold.

norna.c: Norna Norn { Norn (?), Nor"na (?) }, n. [Icel. norn, pl. nornir.] 1. (Scandinavian Myth.) Any one of the three Fates, Past, Present, and Future. Their names were Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld. They are identified with the Anglo-Saxon Wyrd, and are similar to the Greek Moirae and Roman Parcae.

noropianic.c: Noropianic No*ro`pi*an"ic (?), a. [Etymology uncertain.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the aromatic series obtained from opianic acid.

norroy.c: Norroy Nor"roy (?), n. [Lit., north king, fr. F. nord north + roi king.] (Her.) The most northern of the English Kings-at-arms. See King-at-arms, under King.

norse.c: Norse Norse (nôrs), prop. a. [Dan. Norsk, fr. nord north. See North.] Of or pertaining to ancient Scandinavia, or to the language spoken by its inhabitants.
Norse Norse, prop. n. The Norse language.

norseman.c: Norseman Norse"man (?), prop. n.; pl. Norsemen (?). One of the ancient Scandinavians; a Northman.

nortelry.c: Nortelry Nor"tel*ry (?), n. [Cf. Nurture.] Nurture; education; culture; bringing up. [Obs.]

north.c: North North (nôrth), n. [AS. norð; akin to D. noord, G., Sw., & Dan. nord, Icel. norðr. Cf. Norman, Norse.]
North North, a. Lying toward the north; situated at the north, or in a northern direction from the point of observation or reckoning; proceeding toward the north, or coming from the north.
North North, v. i. To turn or move toward the north; to veer from the east or west toward the north.
North Star State North Star State. Minnesota; -- a nickname.

northeast.c: Northeast North`east" (?), n. The point between the north and east, at an equal distance from each; the northeast part or region.
Northeast North`east", a. Of or pertaining to the northeast; proceeding toward the northeast, or coming from that point; as, a northeast course; a northeast wind.

northeaster.c: Northeaster North`east"er (?), n. A storm, strong wind, or gale, coming from the northeast.

northeasterly.c: Northeasterly North`east"er*ly, a. Pertaining to the northeast; toward the northeast, or coming from the northeast.

northeastern.c: Northeastern North`east"ern (?), a. Of or pertaining to the northeast; northeasterly.

northeastwardly.c: Northeastwardly Northeastward { North`east"ward (?), North`east"ward*ly (?) }, adv. Toward the northeast.

norther.c: Norther North"er (?), n. A wind from the north; esp., a strong and cold north wind in Texas and the vicinity of the Gulf of Mexico.

northerliness.c: Northerliness North"er*li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being northerly; direction toward the north.

northerly.c: Northerly North"er*ly, a. Of or pertaining to the north; toward the north, or from the north; northern.

northern.c: Northern North"ern (?), a. [AS. norðerne.] 1. Of or pertaining to the north; being in the north, or nearer to that point than to the east or west.

northerner.c: Northerner North"ern*er (?), n. 1. One born or living in the north.

northing.c: Northing North"ing, n. 1. (Surv. & Navigation) Distance northward from any point of departure or of reckoning, measured on a meridian; -- opposed to southing.

northman.c: Northman North"man (nôrth"main), prop. n.; pl. Northmen (#). [AS. norðman. See North, and Man, and cf. Norman.] One of the inhabitants of the north of Europe; esp., one of the ancient Scandinavians; a Norseman.

northmost.c: northmost north"most` (nôrth"mōst`), a. [AS. norðmest. Cf. Aftermost.] Lying farthest north; northernmost.

northness.c: Northness North"ness, n. A tendency in the end of a magnetic needle to point to the north. Faraday.

northumbrian.c: Northumbrian North*um"bri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Northumberland in England. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Northumberland.

northward.c: Northward North"ward (?), a. [AS. norðweard.] Toward the north; nearer to the north than to the east or west point.

northwards.c: Northwards Northward { North"ward (?), North"wards (?) }, adv. Toward the north, or toward a point nearer to the north than to the east or west point.

northwardly.c: Northwardly North"ward*ly, a. Having a northern direction.
Northwardly North"ward*ly, adv. In a northern direction.

northwest.c: Northwest North`west" (?), n. [AS. norðwest.] 1. The point in the horizon between the north and west, and equally distant from each; the northwest part or region.

Northwest North`west", a. 1. Pertaining to, or in the direction of, the point between the north and west; being in the northwest; toward the northwest, or coming from the northwest; as, the northwest coast.

northwester.c: Northwester North`west"er (?), n. A storm or gale from the northwest; a strong northwest wind.

northwesterly.c: Northwesterly North`west"er*ly, a. Toward the northwest, or from the northwest.

northwestern.c: Northwestern North`west"ern (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or being in, the northwest; in a direction toward the northwest; coming from the northwest; northwesterly; as, a northwestern course.

northwestwardly.c: Northwestwardly Northwestward { North`west"ward (?), North`west"ward*ly (?), } adv. Toward the northwest.

norwegian.c: Norwegian Nor*we"gi*an (?), prop. a. [Cf. Icel. Noregr, Norvegr, Norway. See North, and Way.] Of or pertaining to Norway, its inhabitants, or its language.
Norwegian Nor*we"gi*an, prop. n. 1. A native of Norway.

norwegium.c: Norwegium Nor*we"gi*um (?), n. [NL. See Norwegian.] (Chem.) A rare metallic element, of doubtful identification, said to occur in the copper-nickel of Norway. Not recognized as an element (1999).

nose.c: Nose Nose (nōz), n. [AS. nosu; akin to D. neus, G. nase, OHG. nasa, Icel. nös, Sw. näsa, Dan. näse, Lith. nosis, Russ. nos', L. nasus, nares, Skr. nāsā, nās. √261. Cf. Nasal, Nasturtium, Naze, Nostril, Nozzle.]
Nose Nose, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nosed (nōzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Nosing.] 1. To smell; to scent; hence, to track, or trace out.
Nose Nose (?), v. i. To push or move with the nose or front forward.
Nose Nose (nōz), v. i. 1. To smell; to sniff; to scent. Audubon.

nosebag.c: Nosebag Nose"bag` (?), n. A bag in which feed for a horse, ox, or the like, may be fastened under the nose by a string passing over the head.

noseband.c: Noseband Nose"band` (?), n. That part of the headstall of a bridle which passes over a horse's nose.

nosebleed.c: Nosebleed Nose"bleed` (?), n. 1. A bleeding at the nose.

nosed.c: Nosed Nosed (?), a. Having a nose, or such a nose; -- chiefly used in composition; as, pug-nosed.

nosegay.c: nosegay nose"gay` (?), n. [Nose + gay in the sense of a gay or showy thing.] A bunch of odorous and showy flowers; a bouquet; a posy. Pope.

nosel.c: Nosel Nos"el (?), v. t. [See Noursle.] To nurse; to lead or teach; to foster; to nuzzle. [Obs.]

noseless.c: Noseless Nose"less (?), a. Destitute of a nose.

nosesmart.c: Nosesmart Nose"smart` (?), n. (Bot.) A kind of cress, a pungent cruciferous plant, including several species of the genus Nasturtium.

nosethril.c: Nosethril Nosethirl { Nose"thirl (?), Nose"thril (?) }, n. Nostril. [Obs.] [Written also nosethurl, nosthrill.] Chaucer.

nosing.c: Nosing Nos"ing (?), n. (Arch.) That part of the treadboard of a stair which projects over the riser; hence, any like projection, as the projecting edge of a molding.

nosocomial.c: Nosocomial Nos`o*co"mi*al (nŏs`o*kō"mĭ*ail), a. [L. nosocomium a hospital, Gr. nosokomei^on; no`sos disease + komei^n to attend to.] 1. Of or pertaining to a hospital; as, nosocomial atmosphere. Dunglison.

nosography.c: Nosography No*sog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. no`sos disease + -graphy: cf. F. nosographie.] A description or classification of diseases.

nosological.c: Nosological Nos`o*log"ic*al (?), a. [Cf. F. nosologique.] Of or pertaining to nosology.

nosologist.c: Nosologist No*sol"o*gist (?), n. [Cf. F. nosologiste.] One versed in nosology.

nosology.c: Nosology No*sol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. no`sos disease + -logy: cf. F. nosologie.] 1. A systematic arrangement, or classification, of diseases.

nosophen.c: Nosophen Nos"o*phen (?), n. [Nose + phenol; orig. used for affections of the nose.] (Pharm.) An iodine compound obtained as a yellowish gray, odorless, tasteless powder by the action of iodine on phenolphthalein.

nosophobia.c: Nosophobia ‖Nos`o*pho"bi*a (?), n. [NL.; no`sos disease + fo`bos fear.] (Med.) Morbid dread of disease.

nosopoetic.c: Nosopoetic Nos`o*po*et"ic (?), a. [Gr. no`sos disease +? productive, fr. poiei^n to make.] Producing diseases. [R.] Arbuthnot.

nost.c: Nost Nost (?). [Contr. from ne wost.] Wottest not; knowest not. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nostalgia.c: nostalgia nos*tal"gi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a return home +? pain.] 1. (Med.) Homesickness; esp., a severe and sometimes fatal form of melancholia, due to homesickness.

nostalgic.c: Nostalgic Nos*tal"gic (?), a. [Cf. F. nostalgique.] Of or pertaining to nostalgia; affected with nostalgia.

nostoc.c: Nostoc Nos"toc (?), prop. n. [F.] (Bot.) A genus of algae. The plants are composed of moniliform cells imbedded in a gelatinous substance.

nostril.c: Nostril Nos"tril (?), n. [OE. nosethril, nosethirl, AS. nosþyrl; nos for nosu nose + þyrel opening, hole, from þyrel pierced, for þyrhel, fr. purh through. √261. See Nose, and Through, and cf. Thrill.]

nostrum.c: Nostrum Nos"trum (-trŭm), n.; pl. Nostrums (-trŭmz). [Neut. sing. of L. noster ours, fr. nos we. See Us.]

not.c: Not Not (?). [Contr. from ne wot. See 2d Note.] Wot not; know not; knows not. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Not Not, a. Shorn; shaven. [Obs.] See Nott.
Not Not, adv. [OE. not, noht, nought, naught, the same word as E. naught. See Naught.] A word used to express negation, prohibition, denial, or refusal.

notabilia.c: Notabilia ‖No`ta*bil"i*a (?), n. pl. [Neut. pl. of L. notabilis notable.] Things worthy of notice.

notability.c: Notability Not`a*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Notabilities (#). [Cf. F. notabilité.] 1. Quality of being notable.

notable.c: Notable Not"a*ble (?), a. [F. notable, L. notabilis, fr. notare to mark, nota mark, note. See 5th Note.]
Notable Not"a*ble (nōt"ȧ*b'l), n. 1. A person, or thing, of distinction.

notableness.c: Notableness Not"a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being notable.

notably.c: Notably Not"a*bly, adv. In a notable manner.

notaeum.c: Notaeum ‖No*tae"um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? pertaining to the notum or back.] (Zool.) The back or upper surface, as of a bird.

notal.c: Notal No"tal (?), a. [Gr. nw^ton the back.] Of or pertaining to the back; dorsal.

notandum.c: Notandum ‖No*tan"dum (?), n.; pl. Notanda (#). [L., fr. notare to observe.] A thing to be noted or observed; a notable fact; -- chiefly used in the plural.

notarial.c: Notarial No*ta"ri*al (?), a. [Cf. F. notarial.] Of or pertaining to a notary; done or taken by a notary; as, a notarial seal; notarial evidence or attestation.

notarially.c: Notarially No*ta"ri*al*ly, adv. In a notarial manner.

notary.c: Notary No"ta*ry (?), n.; pl. Notaries (#). [F. notaire, L. notarius notary (in sense 1), fr. nota mark. See 5th Note.]

notate.c: Notate No"tate (?), a. [L. notatus marked, p. p. of notare to mark. See 5th Note.] (Bot.) Marked with spots or lines, which are often colored. Henslow.

notation.c: Notation No*ta"tion (?), n. [L. notatio a marking, observing, etymology, fr. notare to mark, nota a mark: cf. F. notation. See 5th Note.] 1. The act or practice of recording anything by marks, figures, or characters.

notch.c: Notch Notch (nŏch), n. [Akin to nock; cf. OD. nock, OSw. nocka. Cf. Nick a notch.]
Notch Notch, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Notched (nŏcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Notching.] 1. To cut or make notches in; to indent; also, to score by notches; as, to notch a stick.

notchboard.c: Notchboard Notch"board` (?), n. (Carp.) The board which receives the ends of the steps in a staircase.

notching.c: Notching Notch"ing, n. 1. The act of making notches; the act of cutting into small hollows.

notchweed.c: Notchweed Notch"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A foul-smelling weed, the stinking goosefoot (Chenopodium Vulvaria).

note.c: Note Note (nōt), v. t. [AS. hnītan to strike against, imp. hnāt.] To butt; to push with the horns. [Prov. Eng.]
Note Note (nōt). [AS. nāt; ne not + wāt wot. See Not, and Wot.] Know not; knows not. [Obs.]
Note Note, n. [AS. notu use, profit.] Need; needful business. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Note Note, n. [F. note, L. nota; akin to noscere, notum, to know. See Know.] 1. A mark or token by which a thing may be known; a visible sign; a character; a distinctive mark or feature; a characteristic quality.
Note Note (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Noted; p. pr. & vb. n. Noting.] [F. noter, L. notare, fr. nota. See Note, n.]
Note paper Note" pa`per (?). Writing paper, not exceeding in size, when folded once, five by eight inches.

notebook.c: Notebook Note"book` (?), n. 1. A book in which notes or memorandums are written.

noted.c: Noted Not"ed (?), a. Well known by reputation or report; eminent; famous; prominent; celebrated; as, a noted author, or traveler. -- Not"ed*ly, adv. -- Not"ed*ness, n.

noteless.c: Noteless Note"less, a. Not attracting notice; not conspicuous.

notelessness.c: Notelessness Note"less*ness, n. A state of being noteless.

notelet.c: Notelet Note"let (?), n. A little or short note; a billet.

noter.c: Noter Not"er (?), n. 1. One who takes notice.

noteworthy.c: Noteworthy Note"wor`thy (?), a. Worthy of observation or notice; remarkable.

nothing.c: Nothing Noth"ing (?), n. [From no, a. + thing.] 1. Not anything; no thing (in the widest sense of the word thing); -- opposed to anything and something.
Nothing Noth"ing, adv. In no degree; not at all; in no wise.

nothingarian.c: Nothingarian Noth`ing*a"ri*an (?), n. One of no certain belief; one belonging to no particular sect.

notice.c: Notice No"tice (?), n. [F., fr. L. notitia a being known, knowledge, fr. noscere, notum, to know. See Know.] 1. The act of noting, remarking, or observing; observation by the senses or intellect; cognizance; note.
Notice No"tice, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Noticed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Noticing (?).] 1. To observe; to see; to mark; to take note of; to heed; to pay attention to.

noticeable.c: Noticeable No"tice*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being observed; worthy of notice; likely to attract observation; conspicuous.

noticeably.c: Noticeably No"tice*a*bly, adv. In a noticeable manner.

notidanian.c: Notidanian No`ti*da"ni*an (?), n. [Gr.? back +? comely.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of sharks of the family Notidanidae, or Hexanchidae. Called also cow sharks. See Shark.

notification.c: Notification No`ti*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. notification. See Notify.] 1. The act of notifying, or giving notice; the act of making known; especially, the act of giving official notice or information to the public or to individuals, corporations, companies, or societies, by words, by writing, or by other means.

notify.c: Notify No"ti*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Notified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Notifying (?).] [F. notifier, L. notificare; notus known (p. p. of noscere to known) + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Know, and -fy.]

notion.c: Notion No"tion (?), [L. notio, fr. noscere to know: cf. F. notion. See Know.] 1. Mental apprehension of whatever may be known or imagined; an idea; a conception; more properly, a general or universal conception, as distinguishable or definable by marks or notae.

notional.c: Notional No"tion*al (?), a. 1. Consisting of, or conveying, notions or ideas; expressing abstract conceptions.

notionality.c: Notionality No`tion*al"i*ty (?), n. A notional or groundless opinion. [R.] Glanvill.

notionally.c: Notionally No"tion*al*ly (?), adv. In mental apprehension; in conception; not in reality.

notionist.c: Notionist No"tion*ist, n. One whose opinions are ungrounded notions. [R.] Bp. Hopkins.

notobranchiata.c: Notobranchiata ‖No`to*bran`chi*a*ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Notum, and Branchia.] (Zool.) (a) A division of nudibranchiate mollusks having gills upon the back. (b) The Dorsibranchiata.

notobranchiate.c: Notobranchiate No`to*bran"chi*ate (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Notobranchiata.

notochord.c: Notochord No"to*chord (?), n. [Gr. nw^ton the back + E. chord.] (Anat.) An elastic cartilagelike rod which is developed beneath the medullary groove in the vertebrate embryo, and constitutes the primitive axial skeleton around which the centra of the vertebrae and the posterior part of the base of the skull are developed; the chorda dorsalis. See Illust. of Ectoderm.

notochordal.c: Notochordal No`to*chor"dal (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the notochord; having a notochord.

notodontian.c: Notodontian No`to*don"tian (?), n. [Gr. nw^ton the back + 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos a tooth.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of bombycid moths belonging to Notodonta, Nerice, and allied genera. The caterpillar of these moths has a hump, or spine, on its back.

notopodium.c: Notopodium ‖No`to*po"di*um (?), n.; pl. L. Notopodia (#), E. Notopodiums (#). [NL., fr. Gr. nw^ton the back + poy`s, podo`s, the foot.] (Zool.) The dorsal lobe or branch of a parapodium. See Parapodium.

notorhizal.c: Notorhizal No`to*rhi"zal (nō`to*rī"zail), a. [Gr. nw^ton the back + "ri`za a root.] (Bot.) Having the radicle of the embryo lying against the back of one of the cotyledons; incumbent.

notoriety.c: Notoriety No`to*ri"e*ty (nō`to*rī"e*ty̆), n. [Cf. F. notoriété. See Notorious.] The quality or condition of being notorious; the state of being generally or publicly known; -- commonly used in an unfavorable sense; as, the notoriety of a crime.

notorious.c: Notorious No*to"ri*ous (?), a. [L. notorius pointing out, making known, fr. noscere, notum, to known: cf. F. notoire. See Know.] Generally known and talked of by the public; universally believed to be true; manifest to the world; evident; -- usually in an unfavorable sense; as, a notorious thief; a notorious crime or vice.

notornis.c: Notornis ‖No*tor"nis (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. no`tos the south, or southwest +? bird.] (Zool.) A genus of birds allied to the gallinules, but having rudimentary wings and incapable of flight. Notornis Mantelli was first known as a fossil bird of New Zealand, but subsequently a few individuals were found living on the southern island. It is supposed to be now nearly or quite extinct.

nototherium.c: Nototherium ‖No`to*the"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. no`tos the south + qhri`on a wild animal.] (Zool.) An extinct genus of gigantic herbivorous marsupials, found in the Pliocene formation of Australia.

nototrema.c: Nototrema ‖No`to*tre"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. nw^ton back +? a hole.] (Zool.) The pouched, or marsupial, frog of South America.

nottpated.c: Nott-pated Not-pated { Not"-pat`ed (?), Nott"-pat`ed }, a. Same as Nott-headed. [Obs.] Shak.

notself.c: Notself Not"self` (?), n. (Metaph.) The negative of self. “A cognizance of notself.” Sir. W. Hamilton.

nott.c: Nott Nott, v. t. To shear. [Obs.] Stow.

nottheaded.c: Nott-headed Nott"-head`ed (?), a. Having the hair cut close. [Obs.] Chapman.

notum.c: Notum ‖No"tum (?), n.; pl. Nota (#). [NL., fr. Gr. nw^ton.] (Zool.) The back.

notus.c: Notus ‖No"tus (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. No`tos.] The south wind.

notwheat.c: Notwheat Not"wheat` (?), n. [Nott + wheat.] Wheat not bearded. Carew.

notwithstanding.c: Notwithstanding Not`with*stand"ing (?), prep. Without prevention, or obstruction from or by; in spite of.
Notwithstanding Not`with*stand"ing, adv. or conj. [Originally the participle of withstand, with not prefixed.] Nevertheless; however; although; as, I shall go, notwithstanding it rains.

nouch.c: Nouch Nouch (nouch), n. [See Ouch.] An ouch; a jewel. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nougat.c: Nougat ‖Nou`gat" (?), n. [F.] A cake, sweetmeat, or confection made with almonds or other nuts.

nought.c: Nought Nought (?), n. & adv. See Naught. Chaucer.

nould.c: Nould Nould (?). [Contr. fr. ne would.] Would not. [Obs.] “By those who nould repent.” Fairfax.

noule.c: Noule Noule (?), n. [See Noll.] The top of the head; the head or noll. [Obs.] Spenser.

noumenal.c: Noumenal Nou"me*nal (?), a. (Metaph.) Of or pertaining to the noumenon; real; -- opposed to phenomenal. G. H. Lewes.

noumenon.c: Noumenon ‖Nou"me*non (nou"me*nŏn), n. [NL. fr. Gr.? the thing perceived, p. pr. pass. of? to perceive,? the mind.] (Metaph.) The of itself unknown and unknowable rational object, or thing in itself, which is distinguished from the phenomenon through which it is apprehended by the senses, and by which it is interpreted and understood; -- so used in the philosophy of Kant and his followers.

noun.c: Noun Noun (noun), n. [OF. noun, nun, num, non, nom, F. nom, fr. L. nomen name. See Name.] (Gram.) A word used as the designation or appellation of a creature or thing, existing in fact or in thought; a substantive.

nounal.c: Nounal Noun"al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a noun.

nounize.c: Nounize Noun"ize (?), v. t. To change (an adjective, verb, etc.) into a noun; to nominalize. Earle.

nourish.c: Nourish Nour"ish (nŭr"ĭsh), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nourished (nŭr"ĭsht); p. pr. & vb. n. Nourishing.] [OE. norisen, norischen, OF. nurir, nurrir, norir, F. nourrir, fr. L. nutrire. Cf. Nurse, Nutriment, and see -ish.]
Nourish Nour"ish, v. i. 1. To promote growth; to furnish nutriment.

nourisher.c: Nourisher Nour"ish*er (?), n. One who, or that which, nourishes. Milton.

noursle.c: Noursle Nour"sle (?), v. t. [Freq., fr. OE. nourse. See Nurse.] To nurse; to rear; to bring up. [Obs.] [Written also nosel, nousel, nousle, nowsle, nusle, nuzzle, etc.]

nous.c: Nous ‖Nous (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. noy^s mind.] 1. Intellect; understanding; talent; -- used humorously.

nousle.c: Nousle Nousel { Nous"el, Nou"sle } (?), v. t. [See Noose.] To insnare; to entrap. [Obs.] Johnson.

nowthe.c: Nowthe Nouthe { Nou"the, Now"the (?) }, adv. [Now + the.] Just now; at present. [Obs.]

nouvelle.c: Nouvelle riche Nouveau riche { ‖Nou`veau" riche" (?), m., ‖Nou`velle" riche" (?), f. }; pl. m. Noveaux riches (#), f. Nouvelles riches (#). [F.] A person newly rich. Contrasted with old money.

nova.c: Nova ‖No"va (nō"vȧ), n.; pl. L. Novae (nō"vē), E. Novas (nō"vȧz). [L., fem. sing. of novus new.] (Astron.) A star which suddenly increases in brightness thousands of times, then fades back to near its original intensity. It may appear as a “new” star if its original brightness was too low for routine observation. A star which suddenly increases in brightness to many millions of times its original intensity is a supernova, and the postulated mechanisms for the increases of brightness of novae and supernovae are different.

novaculite.c: Novaculite No*vac"u*lite (?), n. [L. novacula a sharp knife, razor: cf. F. novaculite.] (Min.) A variety of siliceous slate, of which hones are made; razor stone; Turkey stone; hone stone; whet slate.

novatian.c: Novatian No*va"tian (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of the sect of Novatius, or Novatianus, who held that the lapsed might not be received again into communion with the church, and that second marriages are unlawful.

novatianism.c: Novatianism No*va"tian*ism (?), n. The doctrines or principles of the Novatians. Milner.

novation.c: Novation No*va"tion (?), n. [L. novatio; novus new: cf. F. novation.] 1. Innovation. [Obs.]

novel.c: Novel Nov"el (?), a. [OF. novel, nuvel, F. nouvel, nouveau, L. novellus, dim. of novus new. See New.] Of recent origin or introduction; not ancient; new; hence, out of the ordinary course; unusual; strange; surprising.
Novel Nov"el, n. [F. nouvelle. See Novel, a.] 1. That which is new or unusual; a novelty.

novelette.c: Novelette Nov`el*ette" (?), n. [Dim. of novel, n. See Novel.] A short novel; a novella.

novelist.c: Novelist Nov"el*ist, n. 1. An innovator; an asserter of novelty. [Obs.] Cudworth.

novelize.c: Novelize Nov"el*ize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Novelized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Novelizing (?).] 1. To innovate. [Obs.]

novelry.c: Novelry Nov"el*ry (?), n. [OF. novelerie.] Novelty; new things. [Obs.] Chaucer.

novelty.c: Novelty Nov"el*ty (?), n.; pl. Novelties (#). [OF. novelté, F. nouveauté, L. novellitas.] 1. The quality or state of being novel; newness; freshness; recentness of origin or introduction.

november.c: November No*vem"ber (?), n. [L. November, or Novembris (sc. mensis), the ninth month of the old Roman year, which began with March, fr. novem nine: cf. F. Novembre. See Nine.] The eleventh month of the year, containing thirty days.

novenary.c: Novenary Nov"e*na*ry (?), a. [L. novenarius, from novem nine.] Of or pertaining to the number nine.
Novenary Nov"e*na*ry, n. The number of nine units; nine, collectively.

novene.c: Novene No"vene (?), a. [L. novenus nine each, in LL., ninth, fr. L. novem nine.] Relating to, or dependent on, the number nine; novenary. [R.]

novennial.c: Novennial No*ven"ni*al (?), a. [L. novennis of nine years; novem nine + annus year.] Done or recurring every ninth year.

novercal.c: Novercal No*ver"cal (?), a. [L. novennis of nine years; novem nine + annus year.] Done or recurring every ninth year.
Novercal No*ver"cal (?), a. [L. novercalis, from noverca a stepmother.] Of or pertaining to a stepmother; suitable to, or in the manner of, a stepmother. Derham.

novice.c: Novice Nov"ice (?), n. [F., from L. novicius, novitius, new, from novus new. See New, and cf. Novitious.] 1. One who is new in any business, profession, or calling; one unacquainted or unskilled; one yet in the rudiments; a beginner; a tyro.
Novice Nov"ice, a. Like a novice; becoming a novice. [Obs.]

noviceship.c: Noviceship Nov"ice*ship (?), n. The state of being a novice; novitiate.

novilunar.c: Novilunar No`vi*lu"nar (?), a. [L. novus new + luna the moon.] Of or pertaining to the new moon. [R.]

novitiate.c: Novitiate No*vi"ti*ate (?), n. [LL. novitiatus: cf. F. noviciat.]

novitious.c: Novitious No*vi"tious (?), a. [L. novitius, novicius.] Newly invented; recent; new. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

novity.c: Novity Nov"i*ty (?), n. [L. novitas, fr. novus new.] Newness; novelty. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

novum.c: Novum No"vum (?), n. A game at dice, properly called novem quinque (L., nine five), the two principal throws being nine and five. [Obs.] Shak.

now.c: Now Now (nou), adv. [OE. nou, nu, AS. nū, nu; akin to D., OS., & OHG. nu, G. nu, nun, Icel., nū, Dan., Sw., & Goth. nu, L. nunc, Gr. ny`, ny^n, Skr. nu, nū. √193. Cf. New.]
Now Now, a. Existing at the present time; present. [R.] “Our now happiness.” Glanvill.
Now Now, n. The present time or moment; the present.

nowadays.c: Nowadays Now"a*days` (nou"ȧ*dāz`), adv. [For now on (OE. an) days. See A-, 1.] In these days; at the present time.

nowd.c: Nowd Nowd (?), n. (Zool.) The European gray gurnard (Trigla gurnardus). [Written also knoud.]

nowed.c: Nowed Now"ed (?), a. [F. noué, p. p. of nouer to knot, fr. L. nodare. See Nodated.] (Her.) Knotted; tied in a knot, as a serpent.

nowel.c: Nowel Now"el, n. [F. noyau, prop., a kernel. See Noyau, Newel a post.] (Founding) (a) The core, or the inner part, of a mold for casting a large hollow object. (b) The bottom part of a mold or of a flask, in distinction from the cope; the drag.

nowes.c: Nowes Nowes (?), n. pl. [From OF. nous. See Noose, Node.] The marriage knot. [Obs.] Crashaw.

nowhere.c: Nowhere No"where` (?), adv. [AS. nāhwǣr. See No, and Where.] Not anywhere; not in any place or state; as, the book is nowhere to be found.

nowhither.c: Nowhither No"whith`er (?), adv. [No + whither.] Not anywhither; in no direction; nowhere. [Archaic] “Thy servant went nowhither.” 2 Kings v. 25.

nowise.c: Nowise No"wise` (?), adv. [For in no wise. See Wise, n.] Not in any manner or degree; in no way; noways.

noxious.c: Noxious Nox"ious (?), a. [L. noxius, fr. noxa harm; akin to nocere to harm, hurt. Cf. Nuisance, Necromancy.]

noy.c: Noy Noy (?), v. t. [See Annoy.] To annoy; to vex. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Piers Plowman.
Noy Noy, n. That which annoys. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

noyade.c: Noyade ‖No`yade" (?), n. [F., fr. noyer to drown, L. necare to kill.] A drowning of many persons at once, -- a method of execution practiced at Nantes in France during the Reign of Terror, by Jean Baptiste Carrier.

noyau.c: Noyau ‖Noy`au" (?), n. [F., prop., the stone or nut of a fruit, fr. L. nucalis like a nut. See Newel a post.] A cordial of brandy, etc., flavored with the kernel of the bitter almond, or of the peach stone, etc.

noyful.c: Noyful Noy"ful (?), a. Full of annoyance. [Obs.] Chaucer.

nozzle.c: Nozzle Noz"zle (?), n. [A dim. of nose. √261.] [Written also nosle.] 1. The nose; the snout; hence, the projecting vent of anything; as, the nozzle of a bellows.

nuance.c: Nuance ‖Nu`ance" (?), n. [F.] 1. A shade of difference; a delicate gradation.

nub.c: Nub Nub (?), v. t. [Cf. Knob.] To push; to nudge; also, to beckon. [Prov. Eng.]
Nub Nub, n. A jag, or snag; a knob; a protuberance; also, the point or gist, as of a story. [Colloq.]

nubbin.c: Nubbin Nub"bin (?), n. A small or imperfect ear of maize. [Colloq. U. S.]

nubble.c: Nubble Nub"ble (?), v. t. [Cf. LG. nubben to knock, cuff.] To beat or bruise with the fist. [Obs.] Ainsworth.

nubecula.c: Nubecula ‖Nu*bec"u*la (?), n.; pl. Nubeculae (-lē). [L., dim. of nubes cloud.] 1. (Astron.) (a) A nebula. (b) pl. Specifically, the Magellanic clouds.

nubia.c: nubia nu"bi*a (?), n. [From L. nubes cloud.] A light fabric of wool, worn on the head by women; a cloud.

nubian.c: Nubian Nu"bi*an (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to Nubia in Eastern Africa. -- n. A native of Nubia.

nubiferous.c: nubiferous nu*bif"er*ous (?), a. [L. nubifer; nubes cloud + ferre to bear: cf. F. nubifère.] Bringing, or producing, clouds.

nubigenous.c: Nubigenous Nu*big"e*nous (?), a. [L. nubes cloud + -genous.] Born of, or produced from, clouds. [R.]

nubilate.c: Nubilate Nu"bi*late (?), v. t. [L. nubilatus, p. p. of nubilare to cloud, fr. nubes cloud.] To cloud. [Obs.]

nubile.c: Nubile Nu"bile (?), a. [L. nubilis, fr. nubere to marry: cf. F. nubile. See Nuptial.] Of an age suitable for marriage; marriageable. Prior.

nubility.c: Nubility Nu*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. nubilité.] The state of being marriageable. [R.]

nubilous.c: Nubilous Nubilose { Nu"bi*lose` (?), Nu"bi*lous (?), } a. [L. nubilosus, nubilus, fr. nubes cloud.] Cloudy. [R.]

nucament.c: Nucament Nu"ca*ment (?), n. [L. nucamenta fir cones, fr. nux, nucis, a nut.] (Bot.) A catkin or ament; the flower cluster of the hazel, pine, willow, and the like.

nucamentaceous.c: Nucamentaceous Nu`ca*men*ta"ceous (?), a. [See Nucament.] (Bot.) Like a nut either in structure or in being indehiscent; bearing one-seeded nutlike fruits. [Written also nucumentaceous.]

nucellus.c: Nucellus ‖Nu*cel"lus (?), n.; pl. Nucelli (#). [NL., dim. of nux, nucis, a nut.] (Bot.) See Nucleus, 3 (a).

nucha.c: Nucha ‖Nu"cha (?), n.; pl. Nuchae (#). [LL.] (Zool.) The back or upper part of the neck; the nape.

nuchal.c: Nuchal Nu"chal (?), a. [Cf. F. nucal.] (Anat.) Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the back, or nape, of the neck; -- applied especially to the anterior median plate in the carapace of turtles.

nuciferous.c: Nuciferous Nu*cif"er*ous (?), a. [L. nux, nucis, nut + -ferous.] Bearing, or producing, nuts.

nuciform.c: Nuciform Nu"ci*form (?), a. [L. nux, nucis, nut + -form.] (Bot.) Shaped like a nut; nut-shaped.

nucin.c: Nucin Nu"cin (?), n. [L. nux, nucis, a nut.] (Chem.) See Juglone.

nuclear.c: Nuclear Nucleal { Nu"cle*al (?), Nu"cle*ar (?), } a. 1. Of or pertaining to a nucleus; as, the nuclear spindle (see Illust. of Karyokinesis) or the nuclear fibrils of a cell; the nuclear part of a comet, etc.

nucleate.c: Nucleate Nu"cle*ate (?), a. [L. nucleatus having a kernel.] Having a nucleus; nucleated.
Nucleate Nu"cle*ate (?), v. t. [Cf. L. nucleare to become kernelly.] To gather, as about a nucleus or center.

nucleated.c: Nucleated Nu"cle*a`ted (?), a. Having a nucleus; nucleate; as, nucleated cells.

nucleiform.c: Nucleiform Nu*cle"i*form (?), a. [L. nucleus kernel + -form.] Formed like a nucleus or kernel.

nuclein.c: Nuclein Nu"cle*in (?), n. (Physiol. Chem.) A constituent of the nuclei of all cells, containing protein and nucleic acid. It is a colorless amorphous substance, readily soluble in alkaline fluids and especially characterized by its comparatively large content of phosphorus. It also contains nitrogen and sulphur.

nucleobranch.c: Nucleobranch Nu"cle*o*branch (?), a. (Zool.) Belonging to the Nucleobranchiata. -- n. One of the Nucleobranchiata.

nucleobranchiata.c: Nucleobranchiata ‖Nu`cle*o*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Nucleus, and Branchia] (Zool.) See Heteropoda.

nucleoidioplasma.c: Nucleoidioplasma ‖Nu`cle*o*id`i*o*plas"ma (?), n. [NL. See Nucleus, and Idioplasma.] (Biol.) Hyaline plasma contained in the nucleus of vegetable cells.

nucleolar.c: Nucleolar Nu*cle"o*lar (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to the nucleolus of a cell.

nucleolated.c: Nucleolated Nu"cle*o*la`ted (?), a. Having a nucleole, or second inner nucleus.

nucleole.c: Nucleole Nu"cle*ole (?), n. [See Nucleolus.] The nucleus within a nucleus; nucleolus.

nucleolus.c: Nucleolus Nu*cle"o*lus (?), n.; pl. Nucleoli (#). [L., a little nut, dim. of nucleus.] 1. A little nucleus.

nucleoplasm.c: Nucleoplasm Nu"cle*o*plasm (?), n. [Nucleus + -plasm.] (Biol.) The matter composing the nucleus of a cell; the protoplasm of the nucleus; karyoplasma.

nucleoplasmic.c: Nucleoplasmic Nu`cle*o*plas"mic (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to nucleoplasm; -- esp. applied to a body formed in the developing ovum from the plasma of the nucleus of the germinal vesicle.

nucleus.c: Nucleus Nu"cle*us (?), n.; pl. E. Nucleuses (#), L. Nuclei (#). [L., a kernel, dim. fr. nux, nucis, nut. Cf. Newel post.]

nucula.c: Nucula ‖Nu"cu*la (?), n. [L., little nut, dim. of nux, nucis, a nut.] (Zool.) A genus of small marine bivalve shells, having a pearly interior.

nucule.c: Nucule Nu"cule (nū"kul), n. [L. nucula a small nut.] (Bot.) Same as Nutlet.

nudation.c: Nudation Nu*da"tion (?), n. [L. nudatio, fr. nudare to make naked, fr. nudus naked. See Nude.] The act of stripping, or making bare or naked.

nuddle.c: Nuddle Nud"dle (?), v. i. To walk quickly with the head bent forward; -- often with along. [Prov. Eng.]

nude.c: Nude Nude (nūd), a. [L. nudus. See Naked.] 1. Bare; naked; unclothed; undraped; as, a nude statue.

nudge.c: Nudge Nudge (nŭj), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nudged (nŭjd); p. pr. & vb. n. Nudging.] [Cf. Prov. G. knütschen to squeeze, pinch, E. Knock.] To touch gently, as with the elbow, in order to call attention or convey intimation.
Nudge Nudge (?), n. A gentle push, or jog, as with the elbow.

nudibrachiate.c: Nudibrachiate Nu`di*brach"i*ate (?), a. [L. nudus naked + brachium an arm.] (Zool.) Having tentacles without vibratile cilia. Carpenter.

nudibranch.c: Nudibranch Nu"di*branch (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Nudibranchiata. -- n. One of the Nudibranchiata.

nudibranchiata.c: Nudibranchiata ‖Nu`di*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Nude, and Branchia.] (Zool.) A division of opisthobranchiate mollusks, having no shell except while very young. The gills are naked and situated upon the back or sides. See Ceratobranchia.

nudibranchiate.c: Nudibranchiate Nu`di*bran"chi*ate (?), a. & n. (Zool.) Same as Nudibranch.

nudicaul.c: Nudicaul Nu"di*caul (?), a. [L. nudus naked + caulis stem.] (Bot.) Having the stems leafless.

nudification.c: Nudification Nu`di*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. nudus naked + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.] The act of making nude.

nudity.c: Nudity Nu"di*ty (?), n.; pl. Nudities (#). [Cf. F. nudité.] 1. The quality or state of being nude; nakedness.

nudum.c: Nudum pactum ‖Nu"dum pac"tum (?). [L., a nude pact.] (Law) A bare, naked contract, without any consideration and therefore unenforceable in a court of law. Tomlins.

nugacity.c: Nugacity Nu*gac"i*ty (?), n. [L. nugacitas, fr. nugax, -acis, trifling.] Futility; trifling talk or behavior; drollery. [R.] Dr. H. More.

nugation.c: Nugation Nu*ga"tion (?), n. [Cf. OF. nugation.] The act or practice of trifling. [R.] Bacon.

nugatory.c: Nugatory Nu"ga*to*ry (?), a. [L. nugatorius, fr. nugari to trifle, nugae jests, trifles.] 1. Trifling; vain; futile; insignificant.

nugget.c: Nugget Nug"get (?), n. [Earlier niggot, prob. for nigot, an ingot. See Ingot.] 1. A lump; a mass, esp. a native lump of a precious metal; as, a nugget of gold.

nugify.c: Nugify Nu"gi*fy (?), v. t. [L. nugae trifles + -fy.] To render trifling or futile; to make silly. [R.] Coleridge.

nuisance.c: Nuisance Nui"sance (?), n. [OE. noisance, OF. noisance, nuisance, fr. L. nocentia guilt, fr. nocere to hurt, harm; akin to necare to kill. Cf Necromancy, Nocent, Noxious, Pernicious.] That which annoys or gives trouble and vexation; that which is offensive or noxious.

nuisancer.c: Nuisancer Nui"san*cer (?), n. (Law) One who makes or causes a nuisance.

nul.c: Nul Nul (?), a. [F. See Null, a.] (Law) No; not any; as, nul disseizin; nul tort.

null.c: Null Null (?), a. [L. nullus not any, none; ne not + ullus any, a dim. of unus one; cf. F. nul. See No, and One, and cf. None.] 1. Of no legal or binding force or validity; of no efficacy; invalid; void; nugatory; useless.
Null Null, n. 1. Something that has no force or meaning.
Null Null, v. t. [From null, a., or perh. abbrev. from annul.] To annul. [Obs.] Milton.
Null Null, n. [Etymol. uncertain.] One of the beads in nulled work.

nullah.c: Nullah ‖Nul"lah (?), n. [Hind. nālā, fr. Skr. nāla tube.] A water course, esp. a dry one; a gully; a gorge; -- orig. an East Indian term. E. Arnold.

nulled.c: Nulled Nulled (?), a. Turned so as to resemble nulls.

nullibiety.c: Nullibiety Nul`li*bi"e*ty (?), n. [L. nullibi nowhere.] The state or condition of being nowhere. [Obs.]

nullification.c: Nullification Nul`li*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. nullificatio contempt. See Nullify.] The act of nullifying; a rendering void and of no effect, or of no legal effect.

nullifidian.c: Nullifidian Nul`li*fid"i*an (?), a. [L. nullus none + fides faith.] Of no faith; also, not trusting to faith for salvation; -- opposed to solifidian. Feltham.
Nullifidian Nul`li*fid"i*an, n. An unbeliever. B. Jonson.

nullifier.c: Nullifier Nul"li*fi`er (?), n. One who nullifies or makes void; one who maintains the right to nullify a contract by one of the parties.

nullify.c: Nullify Nul"li*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nullified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nullifying (?).] [L. nullificare; nullus none + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Null, a., and -fy.] To make void; to render invalid; to deprive of legal force or efficacy.

nullipore.c: Nullipore Nul"li*pore (?), n. [L. nullus none + porus pope.] (Bot.) A name for certain crustaceous marine algae which secrete carbonate of lime on their surface, and were formerly thought to be of animal nature. They are now considered corallines of the genera Melobesia and Lithothamnion.

nullity.c: Nullity Nul"li*ty (nŭl"lĭ*ty̆), n.; pl. Nullities. [LL. nullitias, fr. L. nullus none: cf. F. nullité. See Null.]

numb.c: Numb Numb (nŭm), a. [OE. nume, nome, prop., seized, taken, p. p. of nimen to take, AS. niman, p. p. numen. √7. See Nimble, Nomad, and cf. Benumb.]

Numb Numb, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Numbed (nŭmd); p. pr. & vb. n. Numbing (nŭm"ĭng).] To make numb; to deprive of the power of sensation or motion; to render senseless or inert; to deaden; to benumb; to stupefy.

number.c: Number Num"ber (nŭm"bẽr), n. [OE. nombre, F. nombre, L. numerus; akin to Gr. no`mos that which is dealt out, fr. ne`mein to deal out, distribute. See Numb, Nomad, and cf. Numerate, Numero, Numerous.] 1. That which admits of being counted or reckoned; a unit, or an aggregate of units; a numerable aggregate or collection of individuals; an assemblage made up of distinct things expressible by figures.
Number Num"ber, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Numbered (nŭm"bẽrd); p. pr & vb. n. Numbering.] [OE. nombren, noumbren, F. nombrer, fr. L. numerare, numeratum. See Number, n.]

numbers.c: Numbers Num"bers (?), prop. n. pl. of Number. The fourth book of the Pentateuch, containing the census of the Hebrews.

numbfish.c: Numbfish Numb"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) The torpedo, which numbs by the electric shocks which it gives.

numbness.c: Numbness Numb"ness (?), n. The condition of being numb; that state of a living body in which it loses, wholly or in part, the power of feeling or motion.

numerable.c: Numerable Nu"mer*a*ble (?), a. [L. numerabilis. See Number, v. t.] Capable of being numbered or counted.

numeral.c: Numeral Nu"mer*al (?), a. [L. numeralis, fr. numerus number: cf. F. numéral. See Number, n.]
Numeral Nu"mer*al, n. 1. A figure or character used to express a number; as, the Arabic numerals, 1, 2, 3, etc.; the Roman numerals, I, V, X, L, etc.

numerally.c: Numerally Nu"mer*al*ly, adv. According to number; in number; numerically.

numerary.c: Numerary Nu"mer*a*ry (?), a. [LL. numerarius: cf. F. numéraire.] Belonging to a certain number; counting as one of a collection or body.

numerate.c: Numerate Nu"mer*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Numerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Numerating (?).] [L. numeratus, p. p. of numerare to count. See Number, v.] (Arith.) To divide off and read according to the rules of numeration; as, to numerate a row of figures.

numeration.c: Numeration Nu`mer*a"tion (?), n. [L. numeratio a counting out: cf. F. numération.] 1. The act or art of numbering.

numerative.c: Numerative Nu"mer*a*tive (?), a. Of or pertaining to numeration; as, a numerative system. Eng. Cyc.

numerator.c: Numerator Nu"mer*a"tor (?), n. [L. numerator: cf. F. numérateur.] 1. One who numbers.

numerical.c: Numerical Numeric { Nu*mer"ic (?), Nu*mer"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. numérique. See Number, n.]

numeric.c: Numeric Nu*mer"ic, n. (Math.) Any number, proper or improper fraction, or incommensurable ratio. The term also includes any imaginary expression like m + n√-1, where m and n are real numerics.

numerically.c: Numerically Nu*mer"ic*al*ly, adv. In a numerical manner; in numbers; with respect to number, or sameness in number; as, a thing is numerically the same, or numerically different.

numerist.c: Numerist Nu"mer*ist (?), n. One who deals in numbers. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

numero.c: Numero Nu"me*ro (?), n. [It., or F. numéro; both fr. L. numerus number.] Number; -- often abbrev. No.

numerosity.c: Numerosity Nu`mer*os"i*ty (?), n. [L. numerositas.] 1. The state of being numerous; numerousness. [Obs.]

numerous.c: Numerous Nu"mer*ous (?), a. [L. numerosus. See Number.] 1. Consisting of a great number of units or individual objects; being many; as, a numerous army; numerous objections.

numidian.c: Numidian Nu*mid"i*an (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to ancient Numidia in Northern Africa.

numismatical.c: Numismatical Numismatic { Nu`mis*mat"ic (?), Nu`mis*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [L. numisma, nomisma, a piece of money, coin, fr. Gr.? anything sanctioned by usage, the current coin, fr.? to introduce a custom, or usage, fr. no`mos a custom, or usage, fr. ne`mein to distribute, assign: cf. F. numismatique. See Nomad.] Of or pertaining to coins; relating to the science of coins or medals.

numismatics.c: Numismatics Nu`mis*mat"ics (?), n. [Cf. F. numismatique.] The science of coins and medals.

numismatist.c: Numismatist Nu*mis"ma*tist (?), n. One skilled in numismatics; a numismatologist.

numismatography.c: Numismatography Nu*mis`ma*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [L. numisma, -atis (Gr.?) + -graphy.] A treatise on, or description of, coins and medals.

numismatologist.c: Numismatologist Nu*mis`ma*tol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in numismatology; usually called a numismatist.

numismatology.c: Numismatology Nu*mis`ma*tol"o*gy (?), n. [L. numisma, -atis + -logy.] The science which treats of coins and medals, in their relation to history; numismatics.

nummary.c: Nummary Num"ma*ry (?), a. [L. nummarius, from nummus a coin.] Of or relating to coins or money.

nummulary.c: Nummulary Nummular { Num"mu*lar (?), Num"mu*la*ry (?), } a. [L. nummularius, fr. nummulus, dim. of nummus a coin: cf. F. nummulaire.]

nummulation.c: Nummulation Num`mu*la"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The arrangement of the red blood corpuscles in rouleaux, like piles of coins, as when a drop of human blood is examined under the microscope.

nummulite.c: Nummulite Num"mu*lite (?), n. [L. nummus a coin + -lite: cf. F. nummulite.] (Paleon.) A fossil of the genus Nummulites and allied genera.

nummulites.c: Nummulites ‖Num`mu*li"tes (?), n. [NL. See Nummulite.] (Paleon.) A genus of extinct Tertiary Foraminifera, having a thin, flat, round shell, containing a large number of small chambers arranged spirally.

nummulitic.c: Nummulitic Num`mu*lit"ic (?), a. Of, like, composed of, containing, nummulites; as, nummulitic beds.

numps.c: Numps Numps (?), n. [Cf. Numb.] A dolt; a blockhead. [Obs.] Bp. Parker.

numskull.c: Numskull Num"skull` (?), n. [Numb + skull.] A dunce; a dolt; a stupid fellow. [Also spelled numbskull.] [Colloq.]

nun.c: nun nun (nŭn), n. [OE. nunne, AS. nunne, fr. L. nonna nun, nonnus monk; cf. Gr.?,?; of unknown origin. Cf. Nunnery.]

nunatak.c: Nunatak Nu"na*tak (?), n.; pl. -taks (#) (the pl. form Nunatakker is Swedish). [Eskimo nunaettak.] In Greenland, an insular hill or mountain surrounded by an ice sheet.

nunc.c: Nunc dimittis ‖Nunc" di*mit"tis (?). [L. nunc now + dimittis thou lettest depart.] (Eccl.) The song of Simeon (Luke ii. 29-32), used in the ritual of many churches. It begins with these words in the Vulgate.

nunchion.c: Nunchion Nun"chion (?), n. [OE. nonechenche, for noneschenche, prop., a noon drink; none noon + schenchen, schenken, skinken, to pour, AS. scencan. See Noon, and Skink, v. i.] A portion of food taken at or after noon, usually between full meals; a luncheon. [Written also noonshun.] Hudibras.

nunciate.c: Nunciate Nun"ci*ate (?), n. One who announces; a messenger; a nuncio. [Obs.] Hoole.

nunciature.c: Nunciature Nun"ci*a*ture (?), n. [L. nunciare, nuntiare, to announce, report, fr. nuncius, nuntius, messenger: cf. F. nonciature, It. nunziatura. See Nuncio.] The office of a nuncio. Clarendon.

nuncio.c: Nuncio Nun"ci*o (?), n.; pl. Nuncios (#). [It. nunzio, nuncio, fr. L. nuncius, nuntius, messenger; perh. akin to novus new, E. new, and thus, one who brings news. Cf. Announce.]

nuncius.c: Nuncius ‖Nun"ci*us (?), n.; pl. Nuncii (#). [L.] (Roman & Old Eng. Law) (a) A messenger. (b) The information communicated.

nuncupate.c: Nuncupate Nun"cu*pate (?), v. t. [L. nuncupatus, p. p. of nuncupare to nuncupate, prob. fr. nomen name + capere to take.] 1. To declare publicly or solemnly; to proclaim formally. [Obs.]

nuncupation.c: Nuncupation Nun`cu*pa"tion (?), n. [L. nuncupatio.] The act of nuncupating. [Obs.]

nuncupative.c: Nuncupative Nun*cu"pa*tive (?), a. [L. nuncupativus nominal: cf. F. nuncupatif.] 1. Publicly or solemnly declaratory. [Obs.]

nundinary.c: Nundinary Nundinal { Nun"di*nal (?), Nun"di*na*ry (?), } a. [L. nundinalis, nundinarius, fr. nundinae the market day, the weekly market, prop., the ninth day, fr. nundinus belonging to nine days; novem nine + dies day: cf. F. nundinal.] Of or pertaining to a fair, or to a market day.

nundinate.c: Nundinate Nun"di*nate (?), v. i. [L. nundinatus, p. p. of nundinary to attend fairs, to traffic. See Nundinal, a.] To buy and sell at fairs or markets. [Obs.]

nundination.c: Nundination Nun`di*na"tion (?), n. [L. nundinatio.] Traffic at fairs; marketing; buying and selling. [Obs.]

nunnation.c: Nunnation Nun*na"tion (?), n. [From nun, the Arabic name of the letter n: cf. NL. nunnatio, F. nunnation.] (Arabic Gram.) The pronunciation of n at the end of words.

nunnery.c: Nunnery Nun"ner*y (?), n.; pl. Nunneries (#). [OE. nonnerie, OF. nonerie, F. nonnerie, fr. nonne nun, L. nonna. See Nun.] A house in which nuns reside; a cloister or convent in which women reside for life, under religious vows. See Cloister, and Convent.

nunnish.c: Nunnish Nun"nish (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling a nun; characteristic of a nun. -- Nun"nish*ness, n.

nuphar.c: Nuphar ‖Nu"phar (nū"fär), prop. n. [Per. nūfar.] (Bot.) A genus of plants found in the fresh-water ponds or lakes of Europe, Asia, and North America; the yellow water lily. Cf. Nymphaea.

nupson.c: Nupson Nup"son (nŭp"s'n), n. [Of doubtful origin.] A simpleton; a fool. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

nuptial.c: Nuptial Nup"tial (nŭp"shail), a. [L. nuptialis, fr. nuptiae marriage, wedding, fr. nubere, nuptum, prop., to cover, to veil, hence, to marry, as the head of the bride was covered with a veil; cf. Gr.? bride, nymph: cf. F. nuptial.] Of or pertaining to marriage; done or used at a wedding; as, nuptial rites and ceremonies.
Nuptial Nup"tial, n.; pl. Nuptials (nŭp"shailz). Marriage; wedding; nuptial ceremony; -- now only in the plural.

nur.c: Nur Nur (?), n. [Cf. Knur.] A hard knot in wood; also, a hard knob of wood used by boys in playing hockey.

nuragh.c: Nuragh Nuraghe {‖Nu*ra"ghe (?), n.; It. pl. -ghi (?). Also Nu"ragh (?), etc.} [It. dial. (Sardinia) nuraghe).] One of the prehistoric towerlike structures found in Sardinia.

nurl.c: Nurl Nurl (nûrl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nurled (nûrld); p. pr. & vb. n. Nurling.] [Cf. Knurl.] To cut with reeding or fluting on the edge of, as coins, the heads of screws, etc.; to knurl.

nurse.c: Nurse Nurse (nûrs), n. [OE. nourse, nurice, norice, OF. nurrice, norrice, nourrice, F. nourrice, fr. L. nutricia nurse, prop., fem. of nutricius that nourishes; akin to nutrix, -icis, nurse, fr. nutrire to nourish. See Nourish, and cf. Nutritious.] 1. One who nourishes; a person who supplies food, tends, or brings up; as: (a) A woman who has the care of young children; especially, one who suckles an infant not her own. (b) A person, especially a woman, who has the care of the sick or infirm.

Nurse Nurse, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nursed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nursing.] 1. To nourish; to cherish; to foster; as: (a) To nourish at the breast; to suckle; to feed and tend, as an infant. (b) To take care of or tend, as a sick person or an invalid; to attend upon.

nursemaid.c: Nursemaid Nurse"maid` (?), n. A girl or woman employed to attend and care for children.

nursepond.c: Nursepond Nurse"pond`, n. A pond where fish are fed. Walton.

nurser.c: Nurser Nurs"er (?), n. One who nurses; a nurse; one who cherishes or encourages growth.

nursery.c: Nursery Nurs"er*y (?), n.; pl. Nurseries (#). [Cf. F. nourricerie.] 1. The act of nursing. [Obs.] “Her kind nursery.” Shak.

nurseryman.c: Nurseryman Nurs"er*y*man (?), n.; pl. Nurserymen (?). One who cultivates or keeps a nursery, or place for rearing trees, etc.

nursing.c: Nursing Nurs"ing, a. Supplying or taking nourishment from, or as from, the breast; as, a nursing mother; a nursing infant.

nursling.c: Nursling Nurs"ling (?), n. [Nurse + -ling.] One who, or that which, is nursed; an infant; a fondling.

nurstle.c: Nurstle Nurs"tle (?), v. t. To nurse. See Noursle. [Obs.]

nurture.c: Nurture Nur"ture (?), n. [OE. norture, noriture, OF. norriture, norreture, F. nourriture, fr. L. nutritura a nursing, suckling. See Nourish.] 1. The act of nourishing or nursing; tender care; education; training.
Nurture Nur"ture (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nurtured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nurturing.] 1. To feed; to nourish.

nustle.c: Nustle Nus"tle (?), v. t. [Cf. Nuzzle.] To fondle; to cherish. [Obs.]

nut.c: Nut Nut (nŭt), n. [OE. nute, note, AS. hnutu; akin to D. noot, G. nuss, OHG. nuz, Icel. hnot, Sw. nöt, Dan. nöd.]
Nut Nut, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Nutted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Nutting.] To gather nuts.

nut grass nutgrass nut"grass`, nut" grass` (?), n.(Bot.), A widely distributed perennial plant of the Sedge family (Cyperus rotundus, var. Hydra), which has slender rootstocks bearing small, edible, nutlike tubers, by which the plant multiplies exceedingly, especially in cotton fields.

nutant.c: Nutant Nu"tant (?), a. [L. nutans, p. pr. of nutare to nod, v. intens. fr. nuere (in comp.) to nod; cf. Gr.?.] Nodding; having the top bent downward.

nutation.c: Nutation Nu*ta"tion (?), n. [L. nutatio a nodding, fr. nutare to nod: cf. F. nutation.] 1. The act of nodding.

nutbreaker.c: Nutbreaker Nut"break`er (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The European nuthatch. (b) The nutcracker.

nutbrown.c: Nut-brown Nut"-brown` (?), a. Brown as a nut long kept and dried. “The spicy nutbrown ale.” Milton.

nutcracker.c: Nutcracker Nut"crack`er (?), n. 1. An instrument for cracking nuts.

nutgall.c: Nutgall Nut"gall` (?), n. A more or less round gall resembling a nut, esp. one of those produced on the oak and used in the arts. See Gall, Gallnut.

nuthatch.c: Nuthatch Nut"hatch` (?), n. [OE. nuthake. See 2d Hack.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of birds of the genus Sitta, as the European species (Sitta Europaea). The white-breasted nuthatch (Sitta Carolinensis), the red-breasted nuthatch (Sitta Canadensis), the pygmy nuthatch (Sitta pygmaea), and others, are American.

nuthook.c: Nuthook Nut"hook` (?), n. 1. A hook at the end of a pole to pull down boughs for gathering the nuts.

nutlet.c: Nutlet Nut"let (?), n. (Bot.) A small nut; also, the stone of a drupe.

nutmeg.c: Nutmeg Nut"meg (?), n. [OE. notemuge; note nut + OF. muge musk, of the same origin as E. musk; cf. OF. noix muguette nutmeg, F. noix muscade. See Nut, and Musk.] (Bot.) The kernel of the fruit of the nutmeg tree (Myristica fragrans), a native of the Molucca Islands, but cultivated elsewhere in the tropics.

nutria.c: Nutria Nu"tri*a (?), n. [Sp. nutria an otter, fr. L. lutra, lytra.] The fur of the coypu. See Coypu.

nutrication.c: Nutrication Nu`tri*ca"tion (?), n. [L. nutricatio, fr. nutricare, nutricari, to suckle, nourish, fr. nutrix a nurse.] The act or manner of feeding. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

nutrient.c: Nutrient Nu"tri*ent (?), a. [L. nutriens, p. pr. of nutrire. See Nourish.] Nutritious; nourishing; promoting growth.
Nutrient Nu"tri*ent (?), n. n. 1. Any substance which has nutritious qualities, i. e., which nourishes or promotes growth; a nutriment.

nutriment.c: Nutriment Nu"tri*ment (?), n. [L. nutrimentum, fr. nutrire to nourish. See Nourish.]

nutritial.c: Nutritial Nu*tri"tial (?), a. Pertaining to, or connected with, nutrition; nutritious. [Obs.] Chapman.

nutrition.c: Nutrition Nu*tri"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. nutrition. See Nutritious.] 1. (Physiol.) In the broadest sense, a process or series of processes by which a living organism as a whole (or its component parts or organs) is maintained in its normal condition of life and growth.

nutritional.c: Nutritional Nu*tri"tion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to nutrition; as, nutritional changes.

nutritious.c: Nutritious Nu*tri"tious (?), a. [L. nutricius, nutritius, from nutrix, -icis, a nurse, nutrire to nourish. See Nurse, Nourish.] Nourishing; promoting growth, or preventing decay; alimental. -- Nu*tri"tious*ly, adv. -- Nu*tri"tious*ness, n.

nutritive.c: Nutritive Nu"tri*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. nutritif.] Of or pertaining to nutrition; as, the nutritive functions; having the quality of nourishing; nutritious; nutrimental; alimental; as, nutritive food or berries.

nutriture.c: Nutriture Nu"tri*ture (?), n. [L. nutritura, fr. nutrire to nourish.] Nutrition; nourishment. [Obs.] Harvey.

nutshell.c: Nutshell Nut"shell` (?), n. 1. The shell or hard external covering in which the kernel of a nut is inclosed.

nutter.c: Nutter Nut"ter (?), n. A gatherer of nuts.

nutting.c: Nutting Nut"ting (?), n. The act of gathering nuts.

nux.c: Nux vomica Nux` vom"i*ca (?). [NL., fr. L. nux a nut + vomere to vomit.] The seed of Strychnos Nuxvomica, a tree which abounds on the Malabar and Coromandel coasts of the East Indies. From this seed the deadly poisons known as strychnine and brucine are obtained. The seeds are sometimes called Quaker buttons.

nuzzle.c: Nuzzle Nuz"zle (nŭz"z'l), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Nuzzled (nŭz"z'ld);p. pr. & vb. n. Nuzzling (nŭz"zlĭng).] [See Noursle.]
Nuzzle Nuz"zle (nŭz"z'l), v. i. [Dim. fr. nose. See Nozzle.] 1. To work with the nose, like a swine in the mud.

ny.c: Ny Ny (?). [Contr. fr. ne I.] Not I; nor I. [Obs.]

nye.c: Nye Ny { Ny, Nye (?) }, a. & adv. Nigh. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Nye Nye (?), n. [Prob. fr. F. nid nest, brood, L. nidus nest. See Nest, and cf. Eye brood, Nide.] A brood or flock of pheasants.

nyctalopia.c: Nyctalopia ‖Nyc`ta*lo"pi*a (nĭk`tȧ*lō"pĭ*ȧ), n. [L. nyctalopia, fr. nyctalops a nyctalops, Gr. nykta`lwps. Gr. nykta`lwps meant, a person affected either with day blindness or with night blindness, and in the former case was derived fr. ny`x, nykto`s, night + 'w`ps, 'wpo`s, the eye; in the latter, fr. ny`x + 'alao`s blind + 'w`ps.] (Med.) (a) A disease of the eye, in consequence of which the patient can see well in a faint light or at twilight, but is unable to see during the day or in a strong light; day blindness. (b) See Moonblink.

nyctalops.c: Nyctalops Nyc"ta*lops (?), n. [L., from Gr. nykta`lwps.] One afflicted with nyctalopia.

nycthemeron.c: Nycthemeron Nyc*the"me*ron (?), n. [Gr.?; ny`x, nykto`s, night +? day.] The natural day and night, or space of twenty-four hours.

nyctibune.c: Nyctibune Nyc"ti*bune (?), n. (Zool.) A South American bird of the genus Nyctibius, allied to the goatsuckers.

nyctitropic.c: Nyctitropic Nyc`ti*trop"ic (?), a. [From Gr. ny`x, nykto`s, night +? turning.] (Bot.) Turning or bending at night into special positions.

nyctitropism.c: Nyctitropism Nyc*tit"ro*pism (?), n. [From Gr. ny`x, nykto`s, night +? to turn.] (Plant Physiol.) The tendency of certain plant organs, as leaves, to assume special “sleeping” positions or make curvatures under the influence of darkness. It is well illustrated in the leaflets of clover and other leguminous plants.

nyctophile.c: Nyctophile Nyc"to*phile (?), n. [Gr. ny`x, nykto`s, night +? to love.] (Zool.) Any Australian bat of the genus Nyctophilus, having a very simple nasal appendage.

nyentek.c: Nyentek ‖Ny*en"tek (?), n. (Zool.) A carnivorous mammal (Helictis moscatus, or Helictis orientalis), native of Eastern Asia and the Indies. It has a dorsal white stripe, and another one across the shoulders. It has a strong musky odor.

nylgau.c: Nylgau Nylghau { Nyl"ghau, Nyl"gau } (?), n. [Hind. & Per. nīlgāw, prop., a blue cow; Per. nīl blue + gāw cow. See Lilac, and Cow the animal.] (Zool.) A large Asiatic antelope (Boselaphus tragocamelus, syn. Portax tragocamelus), found in Northern India; called also the blue bull. It has short horns, a black mane, and a bunch of long hair on the throat. The general color is grayish brown; the male is blue-grey with white markings, and the female is brownish with no horns. [Written also neelghau, nilgau, nylghai, and nylghaie.]

nymph.c: nymph nymph (nĭmf), n. [L. nympha nymph, bride, young woman, Gr. ny`mfh: cf. F. nymphe. Cf. Nuptial.]

nympha.c: nympha ‖nym"pha (?), n.; pl. Nymphae (#). [L. See Nymph a goddess.] 1. (Zool.) Same as Nymph, 3.

nymphaea.c: Nymphaea ‖Nym*phae"a (?), prop. n. [L., the water lily, Gr.?.] (Bot.) A genus of aquatic plants having showy flowers (white, blue, pink, or yellow, often fragrant), including the white water lily and the Egyptia lotus.

nymphal.c: nymphal nymph"al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a nymph or nymphs; nymphean.

nymphales.c: Nymphales Nym*pha"les (?), prop. n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) Same as Nymphalidae, an extensive family of butterflies including the nymphs, the satyrs, the monarchs, the heliconias, and others; -- called also brush-footed butterflies.

nymphean.c: Nymphean Nym*phe"an (?), a. [Gr.?. See Nymph.] Of, pertaining to, or appropriate to, nymphs; inhabited by nymphs; as, a nymphean cave.

nymphet.c: Nymphet Nymph"et (?), n. A little or young nymph. [Poetic] “The nymphets sporting there.” Drayton.

nymphical.c: Nymphical Nymphic { Nymph"ic (?), Nymph"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.? bridal.] Of or pertaining to nymphs.

nymphiparous.c: Nymphiparous Nym*phip"a*rous (?), a. [Nymph + L. parere to produce.] (Zool.) Producing pupas or nymphs.

nymphish.c: Nymphish Nymph"ish (?), a. Relating to nymphs; ladylike. “Nymphish war.” Drayton.

nymphly.c: Nymphly Nymphlike { Nymph"like` (?), Nymph"ly (?), } a. Resembling, or characteristic of, a nymph.

nympholepsy.c: Nympholepsy Nym"pho*lep`sy (nĭm"fo*lĕp`sy̆), n. [Gr. ny`mfh a nymph + lamba`nein to seize.] A species of demoniac enthusiasm or possession coming upon one who had accidentally looked upon a nymph; ecstasy. [R.] De Quincey.

nympholeptic.c: Nympholeptic Nym`pho*lep"tic (nĭm`fo*lĕp"tĭk), a. Under the influence of nympholepsy; ecstatic; frenzied. [Poetic]

nymphomania.c: nymphomania nym`pho*ma"ni*a (nĭm`fo*mā"nĭ*ȧ), n. [Gr. ny`mfh a bride + mani`a madness.] (Med.) An uncontrollable excessive sexual desire in women, constituting a true disease.

nymphomany.c: Nymphomany Nym"pho*ma`ny (?), n. [Cf. F. nymphomanie.] (Med.) Same as Nymphomania.

nymphotomy.c: Nymphotomy Nym*phot"o*my (?), n. [Nympha + Gr. te`mnein to cut.] (Med.) Excision of the nymphae.

nys.c: Nys Nys (?). Is not. See Nis. Chaucer. Spenser.

nystagmus.c: Nystagmus ‖Nys*tag"mus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? drowsiness, fr.? to nod in sleep, to slumber.] (Med.) A rapid involuntary oscillation of the eyeballs.

nyula.c: Nyula Ny*u"la (?), prop. n. (Zool.) A species of ichneumon (Herpestes nyula). Its fur is beautifully variegated by closely set zigzag markings.
